speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST OF UNITED STATES FOR PERMISSION TO CONSTRUCT STORAGE DAMS ON COLUMBIA AND PEND D'OREILLE RIVERS
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) asked the following question:
In view of recent press dispatches can the Prime Minister inform the house whether this government has been approached .by the United States government for permission to construct storage dams on the Columbia and Pend d'Oreille rivers north of the international boundary?
I was not in a position to answer the question at the moment, although I knew that some weeks ago no approach had been made, and I may now inform the hon. member that the United States government has not up to the present approached the Canadian government with regard to this matter.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN OBTAINING APPLICATION AND RENEWAL FORMS

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln): There is a matter which I desire to direct to the attention of the government, presumably of the Prime Minister. It arises out of a letter, a copy of which I have just received, from the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs. It is dated February 15, 1943, and reads in part:
. . . in view of the war-time necessity of conserving paper and the reduced demand for passports, a new method of distributing passport application forms has had to be adopted.
I rather question the necessity of conserving paper, and I think members of the house will perhaps bear me out in that regard. However, I would point out that according to this letter it is necessary to apply individually to Ottawa td obtain these passport applications for renewals. At border points that is
War Appropriation-Army

a serious handicap. Very often emergencies arise and a person with a current passport cannot rush down-at any rate, I am so informed-and get one of these temporary applications, and cross on a visa, a temporary crossing permit. It seems to me that some medium ought to be established, particularly at points along the border through which not only application forms but renewal forms might be obtained without a great deal of trouble and delay. I suggest to the Prime Minister that his department should do something to facilitate the distribution of these forms, because the excuse about the conservation of paper is something I cannot concede. Distribution should be facilitated particularly at border points so that people may be able to obtain the forms instead of having to write individually. I was told that we had to submit the name of the person desiring an extended passport before we could get an application form. The thing has gone from one extreme to the other.
Right Hon. W. L.' MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister): I did answer a question some little time ago which was similar to the one with which my hon. friend began his remarks, but I should like to look very carefully into what he has said before attempting to give a further answer. I shall seek to give it to him to-morrow if possible.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, May 24, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
1. Civil salaries and wages, $8,832,687.

speakeroldname: Hon J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Last evening I gave some figures regarding civilian personnel which is provided for under this item. I gave the number of employees in the different military branches at Ottawa and in the different military districts. On checking these figures last night I found that there are certain special establishments and activities in connection with which civilian personnel are employed and which are covered by this item. These total 966 persons and they should be added to the total of 7,466 which was given last night and which appears
iMr. Lockhart.]
on page 2978 of Hansard. The establishments to which these 966 persons would be allotted are Canadian military headquarters in London, other units overseas, certain army trade schools, officers' training centres, cadet services and miscellaneous activities.

Mr. Chairman, I shall try to be just as cool as a block of ice. We are dealing with item No. 1, civil salaries and wages, $8,832,687. This is a good occasion to apply my theories on auditing and accounting. They are not new. My argument will be based, first, on the departmental reports; second, on the estimates, and, third, on the [DOT]auditor general's reports. I found I had to do some statutory work which involved the reconstruction of the law in order to know the effect of subsequent amendments. As the reports of the auditor general with regard to the militia branch, and the departmental reports with regard to the militia branch, amount to practically nothing, I shall have to reconstitute the whole thing in my references to past reports.
I have in my hand reports of the Department of National Defence from 1938-39 down to the present fiscal year. The report which covered the twelve months ending March 31, 1939, contained 118 pages. Thirteen pages had to do with naval services, and 16 pages with air services, so that subtracting the total of these two, 29 pages, from the 118 pages, leaves
89	pages having to do with militia affairs. In 1939-40 the report contained 114 pages, less 4 for naval services, and 20 for air services, leaving
90	pages for the militia branch. Seven or eight pages were taken up in connection with general activities of the three branches of the armed services. In 1940-41 the report contained only 39 pages. This was the first year in which the present incumbent was in charge of the department. Five pages were taken for naval services, and 10 pages for air services, which left only 24 pages for the militia. In 1941-42 the report contained 48 pages. Five pages had reference to naval services, 12 pages to air services, which left 31 pages for the militia branch.
The report of 1938-39 was submitted to the governor general by the then Minister of National Defence who is now Minister of Pensions and National Health. It was prepared by the present Minister of National War Services, who was then Deputy Minister of National Defence. I am satisfied with that report. The following year the report was signed by Mr. Maelachlan and Colonel DesRosiers, joint deputy ministers of national defence. The fiscal year ended on March 31, 1940, and the

War Appropriation-Army
Hon, Norman Rogers was killed in June, 1940. This was the last report issued when he was head of the department. These two reports contained eighty-nine and ninety pages respectively for the militia branch, but since the present incumbent took charge the militia branch activities have covered only twenty-four and thirty-one pages.
Let us look at the estimates for some of these years. I have the estimates for 1938-39, 1939^40, and the fiscal year which will end on March 31 next. I have made a tabulation, which shows that for the fiscal year 1938-39 the militia estimates amounted to something over $34,000,000; the militia items numbered nineteen and the details of services covered six pages. In the following year, 1939-40, the main estimates provided a total of $63,435,000 for the militia department; the items numbered twenty-eight and the details of services covered nine pages, though in that year the actual expenditures amounted to $125,679,000. For the year 1943-44 * there is an item of $40,510.42, involving eleven militia items, with the details of services on one page. Now we have before us an estimate of $1,764,000,000, covering eleven militia items. In other words there were eleven militia items covered by $40,000 and now we have eleven militia items covered by $1,764,000,000- Is that a satisfactory proportion? One has only to divide $40,000 by eieven and also to divide $1,764,000,000 by eleven to see the proportion that exists in this regard.
Then let us take the auditor general's report. In 1938-39, when the expenditure was just over $34,000,000, this department was given seventy-seven pages in the auditor general's report. In 1939-40, when the expenditure was $125,000,000, the number of pages in the auditor general's report was decreased to forty-four; in other words when the expenditure was about four and a half times greater, the pages of details were approximately only two-fifths fewer. Mark you, sir; seventy-seven pages in 1938-39, the last year of peace, for an expenditure of $34,000,000; forty-four pages for an expenditure of S125,000,000 in 1940, the first year of the war, and ever since then the expenditure has been increasing while the number of pages in the auditor general's report has been decreasing. You will be astonished, sir, to learn that in 1940-41 this department covered only five and a half pages in the auditor general's report, and the same in 194142. The details were given only in regard to a small amount, approximately $40,000; for the rest we have no information.
My contention, Mr. Chairman, is that there is no possible justification for refusing to give the house and the country details as to the expenditures of this department in Ottawa. If we compare the estimates for this year, 1943-44. with those of 1940, which bear the signature of the present incumbent though they cover the last year of service of a gentleman who was respectful of the old parliamentary tradition of rendering detailed accounts to the House of Commons, we see that only the minor items have been put in. Out of respect to the memory of the late Hon. Norman Rogers I must mention the fact that in the main estimates of 1939-40 there appeared item No. 173, covering departmental administration, amounting to $438,900. I submit that the salaries paid in Ottawa to all those employed here should be shown separately in the estimates; I do not think even the minister should object to that. There were small items then, as there are small items now; for instance, item 174 covers grants to military associations and amounts to $11,600. In 1939-40 it was item No. 189. Then item No. 176 was item No. 209, in 1939-40; items 177 to 182 were items 212 to 216. Two have been added, but they are relatively small, amounting to $40,000. The total in the main estimates of 1939-40, the first year of the war, when Mr. Rogers was minister, was $63,435,000; that was shown in the estimates. Compare that with $40,510 which is shown this year. I submit, sir, that instead of having these estimates appearing in a forgotten copy of Hansard, they should appear in the main estimates. I do not suggest that the Minister of Finance should not table the estimates, because all payments come under his department, but on the other hand I submit that the estimates we are discussing now should appear not in Hansard but in the main estimates.
Now, sir, I come to civil salaries and wages. Last year was the first time such an item appeared in the estimates. We have it again this year, but no details are given. There is no rendering of accounts. The last accounts we have are for the year 1941-42, which is over a year ago. What has happened since, we do not know. The last fiscal year ended March 31, 1943. We will have those accounts only when the next session comes round. I find it is most unsatisfactory to have accounts covering a period so long expired.	.
I come again to the departmental reports. I have been struck by what has been said concerning the item now before us, namely that respecting civil salaries and wages. In the report for the year 1938-39 there is an item

I submit it is something to have the number of employees, but we must also know what they are doing. We must know how much they are being paid. Yesterday the minister said that information had never been given. Of course it has. If hon. members who have been kind enough to listen to me now would take time to go through the estimates for the years 1938-39, 1939-40, and previous years, they would find that while the names of those employed in the department are not mentioned in the estimates, the positions and salaries are mentioned. There is no reason why we should not have that information now.
An increase in the number on the staff is no justification for not informing the committee with respect to the positions among the civilian personnel in the department. We have to have that information in order to redress wrongs. We do not have it any more. Moreover, sir, the detailed expenditures which were found in part M in the auditor general's report for 1938-39, when the present Minister of Pensions and National Health was in charge of the Department of National Defence, and when his assistant was the present Minister of National War Services, covered 77 pages of the report. In that report were shown the salaries of everybody, and all expenditures of the department. That is a point I think should be made now. When the present auditor general was appointed, during the recess-I do not know if any hon. member was asked about that appointment- these things started to change, and the number of pages telling the country about the money spent for each one in the department and for each matter involved fell to forty-four; and in the last two years it has fallen to five and a half pages for a relatively small item of about $40,000. Well, this cannot be accepted. I wonder what representations have been made to the minister on. behalf of that change? What I know is that although there was a reduction in respect of the last year that the late Mr. Rogers was minister, we must bear in mind that he died in June, 1940, and the auditor general's reports were published a long time afterwards, after the present minister had every opportunity to make the changes he desired. And this I regret. I have already expressed regret that information detailing expenditures is not contained in a book which is not private information, which can be read by anybody, and should form a check, and a salutary check, on expenditures. It is a protection for the taxpayers of this country; and this is why, sir, I insist on a reformation of the estimates and on a reformation of the auditor general's report.
According to what the minister said yesterday, his civilian personnel consists mostly of clerks and minor employees. Of course the employees in the minister's office who do not wear the uniform must be included in this item of $8,800,000. He did not give us any detail about that, as all his colleagues excepting those in charge of the armed services have done. Why is there the exception in regard to the minister's staff here in Ottawa and those of his colleagues responsible for the other branches of the armed forces, when his other colleagues-the former minister of national defence, whom I see among the ministers who honour me by being here at the moment, the Ministers of Pensions and National Health, Public Works, Transport, National Revenue-all having large departments, mention in the estimates what is their staff? Why is there any exception for the three branches of the military forces? Can it help Hitler, Mussolini and the Japanese to know howr much is paid to those who work in the minister's office? My remarks apply to all the army ministers, and my praise goes to their colleagues who follow the traditions. How is it that the government has two different ways of dealing with ministers' staffs? How is it that that information is not given to the House of Commons of Canada? How is it that it does not appear in the estimates nor in the auditor general's reports? Is there any sensible reason for that omission? The staff is increased.
At the opening of the sitting, just before I spoke, the minister made a correction, and I congratulate him upon being so precise in that information, but what he said did not inform us regarding those people who belong to the civilian personnel of his department. On the other hand, as I said yesterday, there are precedents for acting as the ministers of the military departments have done-I did not take the trouble to check the practice of the Department of Munitions and Supply; but what I state is correct; I wonder why they have not followed the traditions of the United States and Great Britain, by informing the people of this country of the expenditures for their own staffs. No hon. member will be so foolish as to criticize reasonable expenditure for the assistance of the ministers in their work. I know very well that, if he performs his work conscientiously, no minister can discharge his duties alone; naturally he needs some help. But in order that there shall be no abuse, a check must be made. I remember distinctly that, when one of the war departments-whether it was Munitions and Supply or National Defence for Air, I do not recall- was created, the Minister of National Defence
War Appropriation-Army

for Air said in this chamber that every member of the staff would be appointed by the civil service commission. Was that done? No, sir. And yesterday, when the minister stated that an order in council was in force regarding appointments, he forgot to add- that at least one-half if not all of the major appointments in the three army departments, and probably also the Department of Muntions and Supply, are made, not by the civil service commission after a regular competition, but by order in council. Some of those people may be blanketed in to obtain a pension or superannuation allowance and to enjoy all increases which are given to civil servants who are regularly appointed-I mean, appointed in virtue of the Civil Service Act.
In most of the appointments made by the government, made by order in council without a previous test, there may be partisanship to a large degree. And, as those appointments are made without the knowledge of the public, as they are not all printed in the Canada Gazette, how can hon. members be informed of what is going on? What I want is clear and precise information regarding the employment of civil servants. I will tell the minister this, that in the year 1934, I believe in the month of June, I accompanied my friend Mitchell Hepburn, who was afterwards premier of. Ontario, and spoke with him in the armoury at Chatham. [DOT] On the way back from Wallaceburg, where I had spent the night, I asked him if a large number of men had been hired by the government of the day to work on the roads at the time of the election; and he said to me, "Watch out." The road was beautiful. It was a fine day and the highway required no repairs. But turning a corner I was surprised to see a multitude of men on an elevation about one hundred feet away from the road. Their task, their election task, was to bring that hill down. Each of the men had a pick in one hand and a shovel in the other, but they were so numerous and close together that they could not work at all for fear of injuring each other. That reminds me of the numbers of people who are employed in the war departments at the present time. That is why we have the right to know what these people are doing. When I say that, I remember what was said here in this building, in the civil service committee room, by Mr. Putman, who was then chief of the organization branch of the civil service commission. He was.speaking under oath-I had them all put under oath because I wanted the truth-and he admitted in giving his evidence that one consideration in improving the status of a civil 
servant was the enlargement of his staff, meaning by that, that what was considered was not the work performed by an individual but how many people he had assisting him. Therefore, it was to the personal interest of a chief or sub-chief of a branch to surround himself with the largest number of assistants.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday, when I was speaking on this resolution I suggested that the draftees should be sent to Alaska. Subsequently the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the member for York West (Mr. Adamson) took me to task for my remarks. The member for York West suggested that it was tantamount to saying that some other nation should do our fighting. I wish to assure you, Mr. Chairman, that I had no such intention. I know the member for Lake Centre and the member for York West and respect them highly. I know that neither of them would knowingly put a wrong interpretation on any remarks I made. I must therefore conclude that I did not make myself clear, and I shall endeavour this afternoon in a very few minutes to do so.
Here are the facts. At the present time there are in Canada 80,000 men who have been called for military training under the National Resources Mobilization Act and who have not volunteered for service overseas. By a recent order in council these men can be sent to Alaska. At the present time they are being used largely to garrison Labrador, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and the shores of Canada along the Pacific ocean. I do not think, considering the present state of the war, that it requires 80,000 men for this purpose, and my suggestion is that a considerable number of them should be sent immediately to Alaska.
Would the hon. member limit his suggestion to sending them to Alaska alone?

I am speaking about Alaska at the moment. My suggestion is that a considerable number of the 80,000 draftees to whom I have referred should be sent to Alaska immediately and that as other draftees are called up who do not volunteer for service overseas, they also should be sent in ever increasing numbers to Alaska.

Where
they will not have to fight?

That is the conclusion which the hon. member for York-Sunbury is jumping at. It is

War Appropriation-Army
not the proper conclusion, and if he will follow me in my argument I think he will agree with me.
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury) We will listen.

This would relieve a considerable number of United States troops who are now in Alaska. The Canadian troops, as soon as they are properly trained and equipped, could go into action in Alaska. Those who have criticized my suggestion apparently do not realize that bloody and decisive battles are taking place in Alaska at this very moment. Apparently they do not realize that the islands of Attu and Kiska are both in Alaska and that if Canada took over the defence of Alaska our troops would immediately be in the thick of the fight. Surely that is not asking any other country to do our fighting for us. On the contrary, it is the suggestion that we should do for ourselves the fighting which another nation is now doing. But in this war no one of the united nations is fighting for itself. We are fighting side by side in a common cause. It is an instance of all for one and one for all. If our soldiers engaged in battle in Alaska I am sure they would bring honour and glory to Canada. At the same time it would enable a number of the United States troops to withdraw and consolidate their forces for battle on another front. It would not be more dangerous or more important than the front in Alaska. We would merely be taking over a very important battle front. Personally if I were fighting in this war I would rather fight on any other front than on the bleak and barren islands of the north Pacific. If Canadians are sent to Alaska and take over the defence of that country and engage in battles which will continue throughout the summer, Canada will play a greater part in this war than she has heretofore played. It would be no task for meek or weak-kneed Canadians. The Japanese are a brutal foe, and for us to take over from the United States a portion of the front on which they are fighting is certainly not asking United States to fight our war.
It may be that a number of Canadians will say that we should not attack Japan because Japan is not attacking us at this moment. Surely we are not living in the days of Pearl Harbor. Surely the attack and bombing of Hong Kong ami Singapore, Malaya and Burma has awakened the Rip Van Winkles in this country. There is no use in living in a fool's paradise. Make no mistake about it, Japan will attack Canada
at the first opportunity, and so far as I am concerned Canada should attack Japan first., and it can be done through Alaska.
If the hon. member will allow me a question, Canada was one of the first nations to declare war on Japan.
I always take pride in that.
Yes, you do, but faith without works availeth nothing. What have we done to fight Japan?

I am now suggesting one way in which we can fight Japan. As I stated at the outset, I knew before I concluded that the hon. member for York-Sunbury would agree with me that we should fight Japan as soon as possible. Of course, it is quite possible that the United States will not want to step out of Alaska. It is a natural pathway from the orient to Canada and eventually to the United States. It may be that owing to the importance of that front the United States might desire to continue the conduct of the war in that area. If it takes that attitude, I suggest to the Minister of National Defence that Canadians be sent to Alaska to fight side by side with the Americans. Our air force is fighting there. Why should not our army fight there too? Someone may ask me, why do you not suggest sending them to Europe. In reply I would point out that we have to-day 190,000 men in Europe waiting to fight. I would also point out that we have a wTar in Alaska which is almost on our very doorstep, and we do not have to wait to go to Europe to fight; we can enter the combat almost to-day. Alaska is the natural place where Canadians should be fighting. When Australia was likely to be attacked, the United States sent its forces in large numbers to that commonwealth. Australians joined with the Americans and to-day they are fighting side by side on the islands adjacent to and in the neighbourhood of Australia. Alaska is situated geographically, in relation to Canada, just as New Guinea and the islands of the south Pacific are situated in relation to Australia.
If the Americans do not wish us to take over the complete defence of Alaska, why should not Canadians be fighting side by side with them on the island of Attu? I would again remind the committee that we have in Canada 80,000 Canadians liable for service in Alaska. Unfortunately, many of them are under the impression that if they go to Europe they will be fighting for Britain
War Appropriation-Army

and- not for Canada. Of course, that is wrong. They are all intensely loyal an|d courageous Canadians, and I feel they would fight in Alaska and the islands of Attu and Kiska to keep the Japs out of Canada. American and British troops fought side by side and drove the Germans from North Africa. Canadians and Americans can, by their united efforts, drive the Japs out of Alaska, and thereby save Canada from the horrors of the Japanese invasion.

I have no desire to criticize or to interfere with the conduct of the war in relation to strategy, as has the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald). I think the hon. gentleman should be in charge of strategy instead of being a member of parliament. I have great respect for him because he is a returned soldier and all his family have been soldiers for many years past. From what I have seen of him in the house, I suggest that the remark of Lord Salisbury with reference to the Duke of Devonshire a few years ago is apropos. When they were members of the same cabinet Lord Salisbury said of his colleague that, in order to show his impartiality, he would talk one way and then vote the other. That seems to be what the hon. member for Brantford1 City is doing. Last year in connection with the plebiscite campaign that appeared to be his attitude. Indeed, it was characteristic of a number of hon. members. The newspapers had carried headlines as well as advertisements-I know that this is certainly true so far as the Toronto papers are concerned, and it is true of other newspapers as well-and these headlines and advertisements seemed to indicate that these gentlemen would undoubtedly take one attitude in connection with the plebiscite. But they did not. They criticized the government for the same thing about which they are complaining again

military strategy, man-power, conscription, and the question of efficiency in the conduct of the war. Many of us did not believe in the plebiscite to begin with. The Minister of National Defence had been very strong, with some of his colleagues in the cabinet, for a change in the man-power policy, and I thought he did what a minister of the crown should do at a time of grave danger to the British empire. The plebiscite matter caused wide disunity in Canada, the greatest disunity since confederation, and I believe that future historians will record that it delayed our war effort for fifteen months and got us nowhere. It tied the hands of the three ministers in charge of the conduct of the war for that period so that they did not know where they were.
It is all very well to say that Japan is our chief enemy. That no doubt will please Washington, but everyone who knows anything about military strategy in this war knows that Germany is our principal enemy at the present time, and until we regain command of the seas we can do nothing at all. We lost command of the sea and until we regain it nothing can be done about a second front along the lines suggested by the hon. gentleman. I am surprised at my hon. friend the member for Brantford City, because he knows more about military matters than I do, and as I say he was an excellent soldier in the last war. He seems to forget, however, that the winning of the war is the only issue before us at the present time. This is the first, last and only question for us to settle. Neither victory nor any amount of planning will ever bring about the millennium. There are too many red herrings being drawn across the trail to-day. For instance, we have heard a great deal of talk about social security. We find that ninety per cent of the talk everywhere has to do with social planning, but surely it must be obvious that social planning and social security will mean nothing at all to us unless we win the war. Why have we all these red herrings across the trail? Why should the attention of the house and of the country be diverted from the consideration of the grave danger that faces us in 1943? After all, 1943 is the most serious year ahead of us. Hitler is far from beaten, and I think the same is true of the morale of the German people. Wars are won by soldiers, sailors and airmen, and not by controls and subcontrols and planners and muddlers or by radio, or by information bureaus and bureaucrats.
We changed the regulations of a year or two ago as to discussion of the appropriation bill and I suggest, in view of the discussion that took place in the house last session, that we would have got on very much better, and the ministers would have been further ahead with their estimates, if we had stuck to the old system on this measure. Very few members on this side of the house, at any rate, would have spoken in connection with the army, and I think it would have been better to stick to the old plan. Members of parliament get only one chance a year to discuss these matters when the army estimates are under consideration. The minister is bearing the 'brunt of the discussion regarding the army. I have no desire to roam all over the place, in discussing these items, as some have done in this debate, but I would point out that all this talk about planning is futile unless we do something to win the war. In January, February and March all

the people in England, and members of parliament, except for ten per cent, thought that the war was over and that Britain would find herself without a plan of social security. We thought the same thing here. What .was the result? We had proposals in connection with social planning and all that kind of thing, but we should leave it until Germany is beaten. An attempt has been made to prevent fair discussion of the most important thing- the estimates of the war ministers.
I may say to my hon. friend the member for Brantford City that I do not believe in all this adjacent territory home defence policy of the government. Why should our more experienced troops play second fiddle in Alaska to the United States forces? Some of our soldiers have been in arms for three or four years; they have had the necessary training. In my opinion the proposal is ridiculous. Washington was not ready for the war. The position of the American troops, even in the African campaign, which is good, comparatively speaking, reminded me of the position of the British troops about the time of Dunkirk. I can tell you this, that this "adjacent" policy is just camouflage for home defence, and there is no such thing as home defence. Norway found that out; they were not prepared. Little Denmark had about 250 men; of what avail was "home defence" to them? Belgium and Holland went through a similar experience, followed by France. Every country in Europe has learned by bitter experience, that there is no such things as home defence against the mechanized forces of the axis powers.
I have no objection to planning; I am in favour of it; but I believe we should not sidetrack the conduct and the winning of the war, which is the main thing. Remember that the war is far from being won so far as Canada is concerned. After the last war we threw away our defences and also threw away our friends and lost two former allies. Many hon. members opposite, and some on this side, believed in the League of Nations, disarmament, and such fancies as collective security. Well, there was no such thing as collective security. Britain, after a period of disarmament, faced insult, risked invasion and later almost extinction. The policy of the government here seems to be, instead of going to fight Germany in Europe and every other place we can find the enemy, to defend adjacent territories-Labrador, Newfoundland, Alaska and the rest. The hon. member for Brantford was not the gentleman who started this idea; it was the minister to Australia who began it. Mr. Davis, in his first speech in Australia, said that Japan, not Germany, was our main enemy. Japan is not
our main enemy; she is one of our enemies, and one of the dirtiest fighters the world has ever seen; her practices are intolerable.
If the policy of the government is to send men to Alaska to fight, we might just as well not look for recruits at all, even draftees. The policy about which the hon. member for Brantford City is so enthusiastic was started at Washington and pursued at Casablanca. It was tried out in Iceland. We sent troops to adjacent territories all along the United States seaboard. It wras disclosed during a debate in the British House of Commons on the appropriation bill that Canada had some men to prevent a strike down in Jamaica. I can give the minister the citation from Hansard if he wants it. I am wholly opposed to this home defence policy. I do not believe there is any such thing as home defence. The moment we lose overseas to Germany we may expect the enemy to cross the Atlantic. I asked in 1937, when I urged rearmament and supported the minister's estimates, if we intended to wait till the enemy came up the St. Lawrence by land, sea and air, and bombed the citadel at Quebec and this building and the Chateau Laurier. Do not let us make any mistake about it; Germany is our main enemy. They are " priorities," as Mr. Churchill has insisted since the war started. But there remains much to do elsewhere. We have seen what happened in the far east, at Singapore, Hong Kong and many other places; we have read of the survivors of the Repulse and the Prince of Wales being marched, as they arrived, off to internment camps. The battle in the Pacific has not been forgotten. United States naval and air forces have done splendid work there, assisted very largely by the men of the sister dominions of Australia and New Zealand. When North America has produced the necessary ships we shall regain command of the sea, and thus, I think, the difficulty to which the hon. member for Brantford City alluded will be overcome.
The subject of civil salaries and wages has been referred to. Large increases are shown, for which explanations have been given to parliament in the last few days. One matter of complaint in connection with the Department of National Defence is the state of the records branch. During the victory loan campaign we knew day by day how much money was being subscribed in each municipality throughout Canada, but in the records office the system seems no better than it was in the last war, with the result that a municipality is not able to find out how many men enlisted from its

Army

own district, and is to that extent handicapped in preparing to deal with post-war unemployment.
I find that there is a contest on between the civil service commission and the three defence departments. A return by the Department of National Defence for Air shows that about four hundred civilians were engaged for service in that department in the Toronto district over the head of the civil service commission -the same system extends throughout the armed services-but the civil service commission had very little to do with the appointments. We have dual control.
Another matter to which I would draw attention in connection with this vote is the inequalities of pay. Why should men who have been over in Egypt or in England for nearly four years get only $1.30 per day, the same pay which is given to those who will not leave Canada at all, or who have proceeded no farther than Labrador? We had a return last session on this subject. I admit that the minister went to a great deal of trouble to supply information relating to the army, the navy and the air force rates of pay. The return started with the pay of a private, and went across the page, giving the pay of a second lieutenant, a lieutenant, a captain, a major, a colonel, with subsistence and all other allowances, and the total for the year, and- the same information relative to the naval and air forces. I look on the duties of the citizen in our citizen's army as subject to the same principle in war as in peace; it is something like jury service. There should be an increase in the pay of the private. Why should one man receive $1.30 a day, while somebody else, because he has taken an officer's course, gets four, five or ten dollars a day? There is a great deal of dissatisfaction on account of the variations, injustices and inequalities in the pay of our forces as between those overseas and those at home.
As regards dependents' allowances, I have received a great many letters written by soldiers in the old country who were on the first item and are now in the second, saying that they have not received the small allowance or cost-of-living bonus which was made last fall under the bonus system. Why some get it and others do not, I do not know. There are also complaints from men who are overseas. A young soldier who has been over for three years writes me that it is a funny thing that some of them have not got the allowance yet, while others, who had been overseas only a few days, were drawing the extra pay and officers could refuse to 
allow it. Much hardship has been caused by this delay, both at home and overseas. This grievance should be remedied at once.
If we are to have a citizen army let us have a citizen army, and let us have civilian inquests. If a fatality occurs to a man who is in section 1 or 2, there should be a civilian inquest. Why should the soldier lose his civilian rights because he joins the army? Are not the parents entitled to know how a man died, with at least the same amount of information and according to the same procedure as if he were killed overseas?
There is another matter I should like to mention. When a soldier enlists he is required to place on his attestation papers the religious denomination to which he belongs. Surely there can be no objection to that; that is the law of England. Yet the department here seems to have some difficulty in giving any figures in that connection. For another thing, many of these young soldiers, instead of being trained for overseas service, are kept at home to shovel snow around the union station and do work of that kind. Is that the way to win the war? If we are to have equality of sacrifice and service and treatment our soldiers should not be expected to undertake duties of that kind, which keep them away from their military training. Further I believe that the out of pocket expenses which are paid the people in this department while they are absent from Ottawa should be indicated in these estimates. It is said that the travelling expenses vary with the rank. Well, does it include drawing rooms on the trains, meals, hotel expenses, taxicabs, other incidentals and all that sort of thing? I do not believe in being small about any of these things, far from it; but I believe a return of those expenses should be made. We all know that these men are working day and night, Sundays and holidays. I do not know of anyone who would want to work as the minister and many of his staff must work. I have a great deal of sympathy for them, and I am not complaining about this matter, but I believe there should be some return made giving more information about liaison officers.
Then I submit that there should be relaxation of the fifty mile rule in connection with buses. If soldiers want to travel to their homes at Easter or other holidays or seasons of the year, they should be provided with transportation. If necessary let the civilians stay at home. Our two railways are making more money now than ever before in their history, yet I have seen some of our soldiers in troop trains which in my opinion were not fit for human occupation. Since the railways are

War Appropriation-Army
earning these fabulous sums of money, to the end of 1940 they made more than they did in the four years of the last war-they should give better service to our soldiers. Then each soldier should be given a life insurance policy, which would provide for his dependents both during and after the war. I have had a resolution dealing with this matter on the order paper since the beginning of the war. Then provision should be made for local carfare for these men. Why should soldiers have to pay carfare to and from the cities near which the camps are located? Some provision should be made for that. During the last war many of our cities and towns allowed soldiers to ride free. Even to-day they are allowed to ride free in Detroit and almost all the larger cities in the United States, but in Canada they are charged carfare all the time. I should like to see soldiers given lower rates or free transportation on the railways. I want to be fair; the minister has made some progress in this regard, as to cheaper fares and meals for soldiers, and I hope he may continue to do so, because I believe it would have a good effect on soldiers and civilians alike. I repeat that there should be some relaxation of the fifty mile bus rule. I had a hand in starting the operation of buses in Ontario when the city of Toronto took over the street railway; we obtained legislation which permitted us to operate buses, and then they began to travel all over the province and into the United States. We have buses for the civilians, and in my opinion there should be special buses to take the soldiers back to Camp Borden, instead of dumping them off at Stroud, ten or twelve miles away from Borden, while the buses go to the end of the line empty and return, using just as much rubber and gasoline as though they had carried the soldiers the whole distance to camp. That is all wrong, and should be changed.
The other day the hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned the veterans' guard, and complained because many of them had been sent outside their own province. He is an old soldier himself and knows what this means. The same thing has happened in my constituency; some men have been sent as far away as British Columbia, which means they can get home only about once a year. In- my opinion it would be much better to keep these veterans in their own province, which- they know something about and where they will give much better service. Already this session I have referred to the cost-of-living bonus. Something has been done in that connection, but now it is only charity and it
applies to only about ten per cent of the soldiers. It is not paid to sergeants or noncommissioned officers, and as far as I can find out, it is not paid to very many others. I hope there may be some revision of the order so that it may be given to all non-commissioned officers and men, and- so that their dependents may get it more directly. Another thing the soldiers complain about is the lack of a moratorium to protect their families from foreclosure and eviction, together with certain other immunities from debt, during the period of the war and for six months after, as well as the lack of adequate housing for themselves and their families. The things that are going on to-day along this line should not be allowed. Down in Washington they passed an act protecting their soldiers, the Sparkman Act, based largely upon what was done here in Canada during the'last war. I understand that the three defence ministers have taken up this matter, along with the minister of pensions; I have had some correspondence with- the four ministers in regard to the situation, but not very much has been done. During the last war nearly all the provinces had legislation of this kind, and I agree that it has to do very largely with property and civil rights, which are under the jurisdiction of the provinces. The matter has been under review, and the ministers hope something may be done, but so far I think only Manitoba, Alberta and Ontario have any legislation along this line, while I believe a bill is being considered in Quebec. Some people hold the opinion that the provinces have no jurisdiction, because it has to do with the war and militia and defence, but in any case under the War Measures Act this matter could be nationally dealt with, equitably and fairly for everyone concerned.
Then I should like to say a word about prisoners of war. No doubt our men who are held in Germany, Japan and other places get their pay and allowances; I am prepared to admit that the minister has brought about considerable improvement in that connection, but I believe much more remains to be done. The Red Cross has done magnificent work; it has been an efficient and trustworthy agency, but I believe the government of the day also owes a duty to its citizens-because ours is a citizens' army-to supplement the work of the Red Cross, not only in seeing that our men who are prisoners of war get their pay and allowances, and food, their mail and parcels and all that sort of thing, but in addition doing their utmost in regard to this infamous, crued and barbarous shackling which has been carried on by Germany so extensively,
War Appropriation-Army

if one is to judge the comments which have been appearing in the newspapers for some time past. I believe the government should keep the people at home well informed as to the conduct and progress of the war. We have a large number of press officers, but I am not at all satisfied with what is being done, and I believe many people throughout the country agree that we do not need many of these gentlemen who, though far from the scene of battle and knowing very little about what is going on, travel across Canada from coast to coast making radio addresses which bring very little comfort to those at home, especially when later it is found that some of the information they give is not correct.
I should like to say a word with regard to the chaplain service. Most of it has been most praiseworthy. We should have a statement on how many chaplains have been appointed in each of his majesty's forces since this war began, by provinces or military districts. We should know on what basis they are appointed, and what is the unit of soldier population set out for each denomination, per chaplain, and who authorized it. We should know the soldier unit of population for each chaplain, per denomination per unit. We should have information as to their pay and all other allowances. Then, are all chaplains who enlist required to go overseas later? What military exoerience is required before they are appointed? Are there senior or head chaplains in each military district, and [DOT]what are such officers' rank, pay or other emoluments? Are they required to go overseas by rotation after a certain period? Are all these chaplains required in the services, for home training purposes, when in cities there are so many clergy not in the enlisted forces, who are willing to help with the work of chaplains, in connection with their denominations?
I do not know, Mr. Chairman, that I can say much further under these two items. I do intend to say something on another item, at some later opportunity. All I can say is that under sections 1 and 2 of these estimates we should next year stop this practice of having alien enemies in our universities in this country. I have seen a good deal of that in connection with the university of Toronto. In attendance there have been alien enemies who never took the king's oath, and who have never subscribed to the test act. They are to be found on the playing fields and at lectures and parades in the king's uniform, in company with our own citizen soldiers. A return has been made 
in the house; in fact returns have been brought down on various occasions, but I can tell the committee that it is against all military policy and against all proper public policy that we in this country should have Germans in our universities. They should not be permitted to meet our own students and have the opportunity of sending information out of the country. That is a totally wrong policy, and one which certainly was not followed at the time of the last war, no matter who asked for it-the mother country or any other country. I know that some of the student body of the university of Toronto feel very strongly in the matter. I do not know what is to become of those alien students in the summer months or what regulation they are under. Where have they gone now? The universities are now closed and I do not know where they have gone. I am anxious that that practice should not be followed next year. Some change should be made. A member of the senate of the university writes to me in these words:
The part I object to is that these Germans march shoulder to shoulder with Canadians in the king's uniform, and if and when they are promoted from the base battalion of the C.O.T.C. into the first or senior unit, they will then be afforded the same instruction as those Canadians who have gone active, and are presumably being given the latest and most practical instructions on how to kill Germans.
There may be an opportunity to mention one or two further matters later on. I believe however that we should stop this planning business until we know the war is won. I do not object to planning-far from it-but I think we should first of all remember that the war comes first. It is of primary importance, and other matters should be considered only when victory is won.

I always enjoy following the hon. member who immediately preceded me (Mr. Church), because he speaks so seldom in the house. May I tell the Minister of National Defence at the outset that I am not going to abuse him. I listened to eighty minutes of it yesterday and another forty minutes to-day, and I will probably get another tody minutes to-night. That is about enough. But may I assure the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that those eighty minutes yesterday and forty minutes to-day do not represent the opinion of any other hon. member in the house, nor do they widely represent opinions in any other part of Canada.

I would not speak to-day, were it not for the fact that as an, ex-soldier there is one point I should like to place before the minister. I want to say here that there is o.ne thing the minister could do to effect an economy in his department. I understand there are two or three hundred on the minister's staff in Ottawa. Apparently he could dispose of them, because it would appear we have four or five military strategists right here in the house who could tell the minister how to win the war. Why keep the two or three hundred?	[DOT]
To show that I make no distinction between parties, I wish to dissociate myself from what was said by the hon. member for Brantford City. Whether he meant to do it or not, he has created an impression which should not be allowed to go unchallenged to the United States. If, as he says, it is the most difficult front we have in this war, why should we send our trainees or draftees over there? He was a gallant soldier in the last war, and I have no doubt he would be in this one too if he could. I am going to accept his explanation that he did not mean what he said-'and we know there are a lot of members who do the same thing. I am willing to accept the statement that he did not mean what he said. But unfortunately the Hamilton Fish's and the McCormicks in the United States will be only too glad to adopt what he has said, and publish it. In my part of Canada at least we are prepared to send the best troops we have to the United States, to back our good neighbour. And we are not sending any troops there because they are not right up to a certain level.
I listened yesterday to eighty minutes of what was supposed to be a representation of the views of one part of Canada. I thought it was a misrepresentation of the views of even, one constituency. I am sorry we have to hear repetition after repetition of it. What a wonderful army we would have to send to Alaska, or anywhere else, if we followed what the hon. member said. He has said that he came from a farming constituency. He did not want farmers in the army; he did not want tinsmiths in the army; he did not want blacksmiths in the army. Heaven only knows what he does want in the army. Having said that, and hoping-and I know it is a vain hope- that we will not hear more from that quarter, at least until eight o'clock, there are one or two things I should like to say.
Incidentally, I can endorse most of what was said by the last speaker-most of it, I say.
I can endorse in its entirety what was said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). Particularly I object to the fact that he stole much of my thunder. I thought it could be done in a more eloquent manner. I am from British Columbia, the garden of Canada, where the minister's secretary likes to visit. I can only say that the secretary of the Minister of Pensions and National Health comes second.
One particular point was mentioned by the previous speaker, namely, the handling of the veterans guard in Canada. In this connection I suggest that if the minister could ever find time he should travel across Canada, not as Minister of National Defence, but rather as an ordinary citizen-he deserves a rest-and come in contact with ordinary people. Probably he would have to get a toupee to disguise himself. He should travel across Canada in the smoking compartments of railway trains and listen to some of the discussions among the soldiers. He ought not to mention that he is Minister of National Defence, but just be content to listen. I see another cabinet minister smiling. I want to tell the whole cabinet it would do them a world of good if they would listen to what is said in the smoking car by the ordinary garden variety of citizen.
We had one company of veterans guard in British Columbia who had been assured, whether correctly or not, that they would be placed! near their homes. I make that statement, despite what the minister may say. They were sent to Alberta and then were moved back to British Columbia. After being in British Columbia for ten days they were moved back to Alberta. The same happened to a company from Winnipeg which was moved to British Columbia, and in less than a month was moved back to Winnipeg. Surely there is something wrong with that. Surely there is no necessity for a movement of that kind. I also know of one very gallant member of the Canadian Women's Army Corps, from British Columbia, who was moved back to Toronto for a month's training in saluting. Then she was moved back to Vancouver to work in an office four doors away from the place she had been working for the previous three years. I do not think there is any necessity for that sort of thing and it certainly will not help with our victory loans.
I agree with one statement made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South in connection with pay and allowances. I did not know until yesterday that every soldier overseas had not received the full increase. I certainly did not know that some little
War Appropriation-Army

crime would prevent him from getting this increase for some months. I served both as a private and as an officer in the last war, and I can assure the committee that I did not think I was a soldier until I had been in the clink twice. It is pure nonsense to keep these men from getting this increase simply because they have committed some minor offence, such as climbing a fence when they have been late coming back from leave. I contend that every soldier, certainly every soldier serving overseas, is entitled to this increase.
What criticism I intend to make now is not made in any personal way, but speaking again as an ex-soldier I want to say to the minister that I think he could dispense with a couple of his staff who apparently were engaged as interior decorators before enlisting. That is the only way I can describe them when I see these badges with "G.P.P.Q.G.G." on their arms. Yesterday an hon. member referred to the patches being worn. During the last war I wore probably one of the nicest patches in the Canadian army. It had a "C.II." with a little inverted V on top, and the colour was a nice blue. From the experience I have obtained from travelling across Canada I know that the soldiers themselves do not like the way these badges and ribbons are distributed around.
I should like to be able to read my speech as many members from Toronto and from elsewhere do. The other day I had the privilege of listening to one of the world's greatest speakers. He never even looked at his notes and he was saying something. That cannot be said for all those who read their speeches. As I say, I should like to read mine so that I will not miss anything. I know this is a reiteration of what has been said-I do not want to give too much credit to the hon. member for Cape Breton South because he never says a good word about me-but I want to say that I was impressed with what the hon. member for Cape Breton South said about allowances paid in connection with adopted children who may not be legally adopted. He referred also to girls who were serving in any branch of the armed forces, in the air force or the navy as well as the army. If such a girl is the support of aged parents, surely they are just as much . entitled to an allowance as anybody else. I think the pay of these girls should be brought up to the regular standard.
I realize that it takes a considerable staff to run the army, but there seem to be a number of men in good physical shape and of military age in Ottawa. You are advertising in the papers of British Columbia for 10,000 girls for service overseas to release troops for the front

line. If we are prepared to send 10,000 girls overseas to release men, surely we can spare a couple of hundred to replace men in Ottawa. I do not intend to speak disrespectfully of the staff here; I think they are doing a good job, but some attention should be paid to this matter.
There is another matter I should like to touch on briefly. At the beginning of the war we were told that no member would be allowed to recommend anyone for a commission. I suppose all hon. members have done what I have done and have not recommended anyone. I realized the minister would not pay any attention to my recommendation and that is the only reason I did not make one. However, I think there should be a little more fairness shown in connection with commissions granted in the veterans' guard. I know of one man in British Columbia who earned his captaincy in the field during the last war and was awarded the military cross and the croix de guerre. That meant something in the last war, and yet this man is serving as a private in the veterans' guard, and a man who, I regret to say, was asked to leave the army because, to put it mildly, he was not any too brave, is senior to him. That is not good enough and it should be investigated.
I sincerely hope that the minister will endeavour to give commissions to some of these boys who have been overseas for two or three years. I realize that the department is training a lot of university boys and I do not want to say anything derogatory about them, but speaking from experience in the last war I know that you will build up morale considerably if you are able to spare two or three hundred or more of these men who have been overseas for two or three years and have them take the necessary training. No one makes a better officer than the man in the ranks who has had two or three years' experience.
I do not want to take up any more of the time of the committee. I assure you that unlike one other member I am not going to speak forty minutes on agriculture and theD forty minutes on something else. I do not think the minister knows much about agriculture. If I have anything to say about agriculture, I will say it to the Minister of Agri culture. I come from a rural riding and I want to tell the committee that we are not looking for postponements for our farmers' sons. We are short of labour the same as any other place in Canada. The reason we do not have to ask for postponements is that every eligible young farmer in the riding enlisted at the beginning of the war.

Following the discussion of Alaska by the hon. member for Brantford City, another question comes up which I think the minister should answer immediately. It has to do with a matter of geography. Attu and Kiska islands are 1,680 miles from the tip of the Alaska peninsula. Actually they are closer to Japan than they are to the north American continent or Alaska. These islands belong to the United States. They are just east of the international date line at the 180th meridian. So far as I can gather from a large scale map, Attu is 172 degrees east longitude and 53 degrees north latitude. If it is the policy of the government to send home defence units or home defence personnel to Attu or Kiska, that statement should be made now. Hawaii is 155 degrees west longitude and 20 degrees north latitude. It is almost 20 degrees nearer to the north American continent than are Kiska and Attu. I criticized the hon. member for Brantford City for suggesting the sending of troops to the mainland of Alaska to do guard duty and to allow United States troops to go on and fight for us. As I say, if it is the policy of the government to send home defence personnel 1,680 miles beyond the north American continent, then I believe the house should have that statement now. Actually those islands are farther away than the nearest point of the European continent.

There was a question I wanted to ask the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) but evidently he could not hear me. He made a statement to the effect that the universities across Canada were full of enemy aliens, that there was no check on their mail going out of this country, and all that kind of thing. That was a serious statement to make, and I think the minister should deal with ' it now. I know that this question was raised at several meetings which I attended in my part of the country during the Easter recess. Instead of enemy aliens being in the universities, as stated by the hon. member, I think the reverse is true. These people are refugees from the totalitarian nations that we are fighting to-day. The minister should clear up this point; it should not be left to go out to the country as it is now.

"Directorate of public relations" appears on page 2978 of Hansard, in the left-hand column, about eight lines from the bottom, and "the branch of the director of information" appears on the same
page in the right-hand column about thirteen lines from the top. Did the minister mean one and the same branch of his department when he used those two terms?
I was talking about the same thing.

Will the minister furnish us with the number of military personnel and the number of civilian personnel employed by the directorate of public relations during the past fiscal year, and show how this personnel was distributed?

Perhaps it would be more informative if I gave the present personnel. It is not easy to speak for the whole year because some are coming in and others are going out. I presume my hon. friend wants the present strength as of a near date?
Up to any date for which the minister has the figures.
I will make a note of it.

Will the minister also tell us how this personnel was distributed by provinces or by military districts, also the numbers in Great Britain and the numbers in the United States? Will he also furnish us wdth the total amount of salaries and wages paid to military personnel and civilian personnel by the directorate of public relations during the past fiscal year, or up to any subsequent date for which the minister has the figures? The use and allocation of manpower have been mishandled from the beginning of the war by this government, which is afraid of the consequences of its own short-sightedness, and which is putting political advantage before the interests of the country. We have only to look back over the years since this war broke out, to get ample proof of the statement I have just made.
First, we had the National Resources Mobilization Act of 1940, with its hamstringing clauses limiting compulsory service to Canada, and within its territorial waters. Then we had the plebiscite of 1942, which I might describe as a scandalous and immoral violation of the fundamental workings of the British parliamentary system of government. Following this, belatedly, we had bill No. 80, passed after weeks of acrimonious debate, during which the then Minister of Public Works resigned his portfolio. A year has passed; the government still dodges the issue, and the man-power crisis which Mr. Elliott Little foretold last November, is now upon us.

I did1 not hear what the
minister said. The shortage of farm labour is principally due to the patriotism of the men working on the farms. At the outbreak of war they immediately offered their services to the armed forces. This number, added to
those who have been allowed to go into industry, makes up the 400,000 men who, we have been given to understand, have been removed from the farms. On May 15 the Minister of Labour stated that out of
700,000	farms, only 4,600 asked for help. No doubt the impression he wished to leave was an entirely erroneous one. The realization of the futility of applying to government agencies has caused the farmer to give up any hope of securing assistance from that source.

I wonder whether the minister realizes how hard some of these officials work for the pay they get. I have no personal knowledge of any military district outside of M.D. 7. The minister gave the number of men as ninety-four, and I did not catch the actual amount of their compensation. I want to tell him that these men work Sunday and Monday, and they have scarcely any breathing time at all. I am not one of those Who are throwing mud at administrative officers. They are soldiers.
No. These are civilians.

Then I am not speqking about the right thing. But while I am on my feet I have something to say to the minister about an incident which occurred in this chamber this afternoon which I do not think reflects great credit upon the minister. I take serious exception to the language he then used to the hon. member for Parkdale. If I interpret the minister's language and his action correctly, he takes the view that no man in this house, layman or other, and that nobody in Canada has any right to criticize the high command; that that should be left to those who have military knowledge. At first blush that statement might seem to have some authority behind it. But let me call the minister's attention to the record of history. I have been a student nearly all my life of Abraham Lincoln, and I recall the days when General George B. McClellan was the leader of the army of the Potomac-a leader who refused to fight and a leader who refused to lead his army into battle. I recall, too, the criticism which contemporary history of that day levelled against McClellan and against the administration at that time. Was that unjustified? I take this view-I wish to state the principle plainly-that, come what may, civil authority must be paramount; that because of that primary principle it is open to parliament, if it is so disposed, and can make a case, to criticize any officer of the army in the course of his official conduct. I am not going any farther than that, but I take a different view from what the minister indicated was his view. I recall, too, that history shows us that when Lincoln called to his councils General Grant to lead the armies of the Union, he was assailed from every side on the ground, we will say, that Grant was a drunkard; and I recall the classic reply of President Lincoln, that he wished he knew what brand of liquor Grant drank so that he could feed it to some of his other generals.
It will not do to say that the high command are sacrosanct. I am not to be construed as levelling criticism at anybody at the moment; it is the principle for which I am contending. Remember the stand of Mr. Lloyd George
War Appropriation-Army

during the last war. He did not hesitate to criticize the high command, nor did organs of public opinion in England refrain from doing so. I think the minister owes it to the hon. member for Parkdale and, above all, to the public of this country, at least to review the language which he used1 this afternoon.

My hon. friend begins with a premise which I do not think he can support. I do not contend and I never have contended in this house1 that one cannot criticize military officers. I have said-I said to the hon-. member for Weyburn the other evening-that I did not myself propose to address interrogatories to officers who were overseas and were very much engaged in what are most important matters, as to the details of an operation, to give them the impression that they had to justify before a board of civilian strategists-I said that-every detail of an operation. That is my position; it may be right and it may be wrong, but I think it is sound, because otherwise I cannot expect and this country cannot expect the best work from officers who are, to use my hon. friend's description of officers in more junior positions, giving days and nights in connection with matters the importance of which cannot be overestimated. That is the position I took.
This afternoon the hon. member for Park-dale went far beyond criticism. He said, in a sneering way, "I want to say just a word about the Canadian army's battle honours," sneering at the fact that the Canadian army had not been in action, when I think he knew perfectly well why they had not been. He went on, "After nearly four years of war they are represented1 by two tragic failures, Hong Kong and Dieppe. They were not failures to fight courageously to the death on the part of the rank and file and the officers in charge of the attack, but they were due to incompetent leadership in the high command." He was not singling out those who took part in the actual operation. He was singling out the chief of combined operations, the men who had to do with that operation beginning with General Montgomery, who was ini the southeast command at the time and under whom our troops were operating; the chief of the imperial general staff, and all those who had to do with making the plans for that operation.
I quite admit in the presence of this committee and to the country, if necessary, that in my reply I was perhaps a little rough, but I felt exactly as I spoke. When I heard the words my hon. friend used in talking about Canadian battle honours, saying they were represented by two tragic failures and that this was due to incompetent leadership in the high command, when I knew who the leaders

were and he knew, because I told this committee the other night, then I said that some day those words would choke in his throat; or in other words that some day he would be sorry he had used them. That is an expression used very frequently; perhaps from the point of view of parliamentary language it was too strong, but it expressed exactly what I had in mind. I felt that my hon. friend had gone far indeed, first when he described Dieppe as a tragic failure; second when he sneered at the battle honours of the Canadian army, and third when he said it was due to incompetent leadership in the high command. I leave that with this committee.

Will the
minister explain to the conSmittee and the country why General Roberts, who led the forces at Dieppe, and, I thought, heroically, has been demoted or, to use the expression which I have seen in the public press, has been kicked upstairs?

Roberts about whom my hon. friendl was talking; it was the high command, and the high command were those of whom I was speaking, the officers I have mentioned.
Let me finish, now that we are talking about Dieppe. I have never said that Dieppe was a complete success, but on the other hand I have not said that it was either a tragic or a ghastly failure, because that would be untrue. As I told the committee the other night, the operation at Dieppe had two major objectives. The first was a strategic objective, which consisted of getting information as to the enemy dispositions, something we did not know and could not get, as was indicated in this book, " Combined Operations," without actually fighting for it. The second abjective was to get information with regard to enemy dispositions across the channel, because we had never set foot there since the days of Dunkirk, when those heroic men left that beach. It was also to test out our own equipment. We had equipment, but the question was, how would it do; how would it go in battle? We had. been through all sorts of manoeuvres, and these men had been trained in the use of that equipment, but would it stand up under battle conditions? Then, it was to test our own dispositions and our own handling of landing craft.
In those respects Dieppe was a success, because it gave us information on all those points, and I am going to quote "Combined Operations" in that regard in a moment. Dieppe, as "Combined Operations" says, was an indispensable prelude-not a tragic failure, as the hon. member for Farkdale says-to further operations. Dieppe was conceived, planned, worked on, practised and put on with that in view. Where Dieppe failed to a considerable extent was in connection with the tactical results. That is to say, it did not destroy the number of enemy installations that they expected to destroy in the area of Dieppe. But Dieppe did something more than that. Dieppe for the first time flushed the German air force; it caused the Germans to withdraw a considerable part of their air force from the front farther east in order to combat our air force. The battle which was fought in the air and the victories which were won on that occasion were part of the gain at Dieppe.
That was Dieppe. The losses were heavy; there is no doubt about that. Nobody deplores them more than members of this house, and I know the hon. member for York-Sunbury joins with me in that just as much as any other hon. member. But that was Dieppe, and
it was not a tragic failure nor was there any incompetent leadership by the high command. It was a climax of operations which are described in this book, "Combined Operations"; small commando raids, getting larger and larger until Dieppe was the climax. I am going to trouble the committee, if I may, by reading not any grandiloquent phrases, but just a plain statement of facts by a man who has become known and trusted, I think, for his truthful recital and truthful appraisal of these operations. This is Mr. Saunders, in "Combined Operations":
In the words of the Prime Minister, speaking in the House of Commons on the 8th September, 1942, "The Dieppe raid must be considered a reconnaissance in force. . . .
What is a reconnaissance for? It is for tb's purpose of getting information.
"It was a hard, savage clash, such as is likely to become increasingly numerous as the war deepens."
If we are going to have ,the people who conduct these operations called incompetent, and the operations called tragic failures; if that is to be the general feeling, I am afraid we are in a fair way to lose the war.
"We had to get all the information necessary-"
Before what?
"-before landing operations on a much larger scale."
This is the Prime Minister of Great Britain speaking:
This raid, apart from its reconnaissance value, brought about an extremely satisfactory air battle in the west, which fighter command wish they could repeat every week."
Then Mr. Saunders says:
The results to which the Prime Minister referred were indeed of the highest importance. Two were outstanding. In the first place we learnt much about the German defences in the west. In the second place, and of still greater value, was the first-hand experience we acquired of the conditions which may be met with in a large scale assault on a strongly held channel port. The details of these experiences must not be revealed. The enemy -will know in due course how we have profited by them. While the Dieppe raid was an indispensable prelude for what was to take place later, in a sense it was also the culminating point in the series of reconnaissances of which some account has now been given. Certain of the results achieved became visible later when a combined operation on a much larger scale was successfully launched; others will appear in the major assaults to come.
The results were purchased at a high cost in casualties. The Canadians suffered particularly heavily.
