Then he goes on to quote the announcement which I made with regard to the number of troops engaged and the number of casualties. He goes on to say:
It is sometimes possible to judge the effect of action otherwise than by the public analysis of such of its results as the military authorities are able to divulge in time of war. Phrases like "synchronization" and "timing" do not always convey the full importance which should be attached to them unless a yardstick is provided by which they can be measured.
Such a yardstick was produced by Goebbels. It was the reaction of his propaganda machine.
That is, the reactions of his machine to Dieppe.
The enemy was very badly rattled. For the better part of a day, axis wireless stations broadcast statements which were at once fantastic and contradictory. Thus they said the raid showed every sign of hasty preparation; it had been ordered by the Prime Minister on his return from Moscow four days previously as a sop to Stalin.
Rehearsing had been going on for that show for months.
Almost in the same breath they said that it was the culmination of ten months' planning of so extensive a nature that the chief of combined operations had paid a special visit to the United States of America in connection with its preparation. A little later they maintained that the raid was meant to be the opening of the second front, a little later still that it was not a second front at all but only a raid. By these and equally glaring contradictions did the enemy betray his troubled and uneasy spirit. The phrase "perfect synchronization," which passed almost unnoticed or was taken for granted by the ordinary British or American citizen, had for the Germans a most precise and sinister significance. They realized that their enemies were able to stage with success a landing on a scale heavy enough to make a still larger combined operation a practical proposition. Where that larger landing would take place, and when, they did not know, but German political warfare, which from the beginning of the war had taken and maintained the offensive, began on the day of Dieppe to turn to the defensive.
The enemy's apprehension concerning a major assault was well founded. Eighty days later the occupation of French North Africa began.
That is Saunders' summary of Dieppe. I submit there is nothing there to justify any hon. member in calling Dieppe a tragic failure, much less to suggest incompetent leadership. That is the reason which prompted me, on the spur of the moment, to say what I said to the hon. member for Parkdale. If my words were too rough, then I regret them, and would be glad to withdraw them. But I must say they expressed the sentiments I felt at the time, which might perhaps have been put in more elegant language. I felt that what I said was justified, having regard to the statement the hon. member had made.

Mr. HANSON (York-Sunlbury); Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to labour the incident of this afternoon further. Perhaps the minister's statement now does him credit, and we can very well leave the incident as it is. Neither do I rise for the purpose of making any analysis of Dieppe. I have never looked upon Dieppe as a great tragedy, except in respect of the severe casualty lists which resulted.
The minister called it a reconnaissance in force. I think if there was failure at Dieppe it was due to the element of lack of surprise, for which certainly those who planned the expedition could in no way be held responsible. It has been explained both here and in Great Britain that the attack lacked the element of surprise. That was due to fortuitous circumstances with which, I think, the British-Canadian command could not cope.
But I am just wondering-and perhaps the minister can enlighten me, as a layman-having regard to the terrain at Dieppe, having regard to the fact that there was a sea wall averaging twelve feet in height, and having regard to the fact that competent observers have said that a frontal attack on Dieppe could never succeed, why was not a flank attack considered-[DOT] if in fact it was not considered? I have been told by those who at least know the terrain intimately, and by others who have some knowledge of strategy, that in respect of a frontal attack on Dieppe the odds were against the success of such an attack. I will put it in that way.
Nevertheless the minister may be able to enlighten us as to why the frontal attack was selected, instead of a flank attack. The theory I had propounded to me was that to be successful, surprise or no surprise, the probability in favour of success would have been much greater by a flank rather than by a frontal attack, -having regard to the almost insuperable position offered, the resistance offered not only by natural defences but by artificial defences as well.
Then, I suggest the minister ought to tell the committee and the country, if he is able to do so, just how far our mechanized equipment was able to penetrate. I listened to his statement the other day, and read it very carefully. I had been told, and the aerial photographs so indicate, I believe, that only one tank actually reached the Casino on the boulevard or the street behind the sea-wall. The minister used the word, "some". The information I have is that most of the tanks were bogged down in the sand, and never reached the sea-wall at all. I am not blaming anybody, but I think a true picture ought to be given to the committee. We ought to be told the reasons for failure to get through. Was it due

IFar Appropriation-Army
to a lack of surprise? Was it due to the fact that the enemy were expecting the raid? I have the idea that probably, being apprised that a raid was coming, they had ample time to prepare.
Then, in the statement the minister made some weeks ago, just after the Dieppe attack, he said that one of the lessons to be learned from Dieppe was-and I must say to him that I was rather surprised when I heard his statement-that Dieppe demonstrated that the gallant Canadian soldiers who went into the raid, who behaved so heroically, and so many of whom lost their lives, had confidence in the leadership of their officers. Although I have not the article under my hand, I think that is what the minister said, and he will no doubt correct me if I am wrong.
That is a rather surprising statement, when one analyses it. When did the time ever arrive that a trained Canadian soldier going into battle did not have confidence in his commanding officers? That statement was on a par with the statement made by the chief of the general staff in September, 1940, before the Canadian club at Ottawa, when he was put up by the government to defend government policy, and told the people present that one of the reasons for the thirty-day training plan was that the youth of Canada had to be taught a sense of national obligation. It is just that type of statement. Did the minister make that statement in defence of the Dieppe raid, namely, that it demonstrated that the Canadian soldier, as good as any in the world, as was shown in the last war and, if an opportunity is given, will be shown again in this one, was brave and courageous, and would follow his commanding officers? I wonder if that is one of the main lessons learned from Dieppe, and why that statement was ever made.

First, with respect to the flank attack, I have not examined the minutes to see what other forms of attack were considered. I can only say to the committee that the plans for the attack which was made were, as I have said, gone over, and gone over, and gone over, time and again. Theyi were changed from time to time, until the conclusion was arrived at that a certain plan was the best one. That conclusion was arrived at by those in whom I have confidence, and in whom I believe the country has confidence. My hon. friend's assumption is a little incorrect when he suggests it was altogether a frontal attack. I presume my hon. friend has in mind that there were two flank attacks on each flank.
The main attack was the front.

Two flank attacks on each flank were planned to take place before the Royal Hamilton Light Infantry and the
Essex Scottish were to land on the front. The two flank attacks on the west were by No. 4 commando-they were to capture the battery-and by the Queen's Own Cameron Highlanders and the South Saskatchewan Regiment who were, among other tasks, to attempt to gain command of the west headland. No. 3 commando was to capture the battery at Berneval, farthest to the east, and the Royal Regiment of Canada were to land and take the. eastern headland. Whoever planned the operation understood fully the desirability of securing the flanks and, if possible, silencing the fire which would come on the beach when the main landing was made in front. I am not going into the details of why that did not succeed.
Hon. members will remember that No. 4 commando succeeded completely. The South Saskatchewan Regiment got in quite deeply, as did the Queen's Own Cameron Highlanders of Canada. No. 3 commando, as the committee will remember, intercepted a German convoy coming up the channel, or the convoy intercepted them. They met and a great many shots were fired. The landing craft were dispersed, and only a small number, I think something less than twenty, of No. 3 commando actually landed. But so daring were they that for something like an hour or an hour and a half, according to the statement of "Combined Operations", they succeeded in practically silencing the battery which they were to capture, by sniping at the gunners.
The Royal Regiment of Canada-this is anybody's guess as to why it was caused; the interception of this convoy had probably something to do with it-landed later than was planned, and the result was that they never captured the headland. In the meantime General Roberts had information, according to combined operations, that the attack was going on; that a landing had been made on the beach and that the tanks had come ashore. It was after that that he ordered in the Les Fusiliers Mont-Royal, and later on ordered in the Marine Corps Commando, which was the second reserve. So much for the form of attack. I have not heard anything which would indicate that the job should not have been done in that way.
With regard to the other statement that was made, when I was in England near the end of September I saw these men, some of them in hospital. I had seen the adjutant-general after he came home, having seen

War Appropriation-Army

these men, in hospital. The adjutant-general told me [DOT] that the thing that impressed him above all else, besides the spirit of these men generally and their anxiety to get back at the huns was the absolute admiration and confidence with which the men spoke of their officers and of the way in which they had been led. It was equally true on the part of the officers with regard to the men. It seemed that there could not have been more perfect confidence and coordination and cooperation than existed between the officers and men at Dieppe.
This is evidenced by some of the deeds of gallantry on that occasion. The hon. member for Weyburn, I think it was, referred to Colonel Merritt. He led his men over a bridge, and reassured them at a time when it was actually under fire. We had universal testimony, not just from the officers but from the men themselves. They had complete admiration for the way in which the officers had carried on. There was no idea of the officers sitting back in a dug-out or in support trenches and sending the men up. The officers were up with the men and the men were up with the officers. That is all I have to say about that. I do not think there is anything wrong in calling attention to it. I certainly regard it as the outstanding feature of Dieppe as it has been related to me by both officers and men.

I do not wish to
make any comment at this stage about the leadership of the high command. As I said a week ago, it may be difficult for us properly to appraise the success or failure at Dieppe. In making his statement the minister went out of his way to defend the operation at that time. We all greatly respect the heroic performance of the Canadian troops at the Dieppe raid. I think of one man, Captain James Brown, who came from my own locality. In order to get over, he went as a medical sergeant, did heroic work and was decorated.
In view of the defence the minister has put forth, I wish to ask some questions at this time. I should like to know the number of prisoners which the nazis took and the number of casualties among those who actually landed. I should like to know the percentage lost as prisoners and as casualties. I should like to know the number of enemy prisoners that we took. Will the minister not say that in his opinion it is just possible that the nazis got just as much, if not more, information as a result of this raid as we did? Is it not true that our people lost operational orders which were captured by the enemy? These certainly

would have been beneficial to the enemy. As a result of this raid we had the shackling of prisoners and other unfortunate incidents.

One can only express
one's opinion. From having talked with those who were connected with the raid, from Lord Louis Mountbatten down, I do not think the information obtained by the enemy was at all equal in value to the information we obtained on the points in connection with which the raid was launched and which would be of assistance to us with regard to future operations. I have heard the idea expressed in the house two or three times, but it never occurred to me that the Germans had obtained information which was equal in any way to that obtained by us.

Did they obtain any
of our operational orders?

I should like to ask another question in connection with Major General Roberts. I have the highest regard for that gentleman, but I wish to ask the minister if it was his experience in the last war that when a high ranking officer was taken out of active service and placed on some reserve duty, this was considered1 as a promotion. Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to discuss the Dieppe operations again. I have asked questions about it and have expressed my views upon it on two occasions, and I do not think it necessary for me to go over it again, except to say that while I agree with the minister as to the value of the experience gained, I cannot altogether agree with him with reference to the second value he pointed out, namely, knowledge of the disposition of enemy troops. The disposition of enemy troops will vary from week to week and from month to month, and any information about enemy dispositions last fall will not likely be of much value in the event of an invasion of the continent this summer.

I mean disposition of
enemy defences, not simply troops-the siting of anti-aircraft and other guns, for instance. That is what I was talking about.

I would say the same thing of that, too, to a lesser extent, because the enemy disposition of its defences, mortars and artillery will change. But the operation did show two things. It showed enemy technique, the methods they intended to employ in repulsing an invasion. That is valuable. It also showed the particular types of weapon which the enemy used with great effectiveness. I talked with some of the men who came back from Dieppe, and they were particularly impressed with the German use of the mortar. From w'hat I have gathered from some of the men who came back, changes have been made in training among our own troops with respect to that weapon on account of the effective use which the Germans made
of it. There is no doubt that this experience which the men gained will be of tremendous value in any future operations.
I am sure that the minister cannot be altogether serious when he says that if we are to have criticism of the high command or of the men who plan the operations, we certainly shall lose the war.
I did not say that.

I may not be quoting the minister exactly. Let me put it in this way. I think what he had in mind was that if derogatory statements were made about the high command-I am not one of those who said that Dieppe was a tragic failure-it would have a detrimental effect. I have not discussed Dieppe publicly outside the house. I have spoken of it inside the house and said that in my opinion the Dieppe operation was not an unqualified success. I am not keen about discussing these matters publicly in war time. But there is a value in discussing in this house the extent to which there is proper co-ordination between the services with a view to guaranteeing the maximum possible success with an absolute minimum of casualties. I think the criticism in this house of the Hong Kong expedition, for instance, had some value because, as the minister himself said in the debate, following that criticism changes were made in the general staff, particularly in ordnance, and I think, a good deal of that came about as a result of criticism in various parts of the country. Men in high positions in the armed services who are charged with the disposition of our troops and upon whose judgment will depend the lives of the sons of citizens of Canada ought to feel that our eyes are upon them and that, while we may pardon errors in judgment, this house will not forgive and the minister will not condone any carelessness or negligence or any lack in the essential planning that goes to make a successful operation. I do not think it is a bad thing for the high military authorities to feel that we are watching them. I think it would be bad for us to be too sweeping in our condemnation. I think it would be wrong for us to criticize without at the same time giving credit where credit is due. But I can think of no greater service which this house can do for the minister and which the minister can do for the country than to make those who are responsible feel that we are watching them with concern, for, after all, there has been given into their hands the lives of young Canadians, Canada's most precious possession.

My hon. friend must not ask people to withdraw things they heard. I would ask the minister a question arising out of what he said a few moments ago when he was telling the committee how much experience our troops had gained at Dieppe and how beneficial that experience would be to them in future operations. With that I agree. I think they would gain a good deal of experience. We have read in the newspapers quite frequently that the Canadian troops now in England are to be the spearhead of any attack on Europe, and I have often asked myself how effective they can be without having had' any previous actual battle experience. That question is prompted by the minister's statement that much experience was gained through the attack on Dieppe. I know that when the Canadians get into the war actively in the army, in battle line, they will give as good an account of themselves in this war as they did in the last. There are no better soldiers in the world. But I would be sorry to see them thrown as the spearhead into battle without previous battle experience. Can the minister say whether they will be thrown into battle as the spearhead without previous experience of that kind?

All I can say is that troops cannot get battle experience without being in battle. That is trite; but at the same time it is true, and the question is, what place you are to select to put them into battle? If my hon. friend suggests that there is some sort of pre-battle-
I have read the statement by General McNaughton that they would be the spearhead. How can they be the spearhead without battle experience?

The hon. member says
they should have battle experience, and he realizes they have to go into battle to get battle experience. In other words, troops have to go into actual combat where they can get such experience. Whether they go into battle as an army is another matter, and perhaps that is what the hon. member has in mind. You cannot possibly have battle experience without going into battle. There must be a first time for all troops. A good many of us have had that experience. I only say to my hon. friend, as I said this afternoon, in answer to the hon. member for Parkdale, that I invite all hon. members to suggest where, up to date, we would have

War Appropriation-Army
put our men in for battle experience. I mentioned some of the actions that have taken place. I mentioned Narvik, and I asked, did anyone here feel that we should have put them there, or that they should have been at Dunkirk, or that we should have insisted upon throwing them into Greece or Crete or in Egypt, when the troops were driven back? I am sure the committee would say, no; we do not want that. It comes to this, therefore, that we want them to have battle experience, but we want to be sure that they are in a successful show. Well, you cannot pick and choose in that respect. Dieppe gave battle experience and there has been a good deal of criticism of it; why? Because it was not wholly successful. I am afraid the government and the commanders cannot always pick the operation in which there can be an absolute guarantee of success, and I simply say to the hon. member that no one is more alive to the desirability of having battle experience than is General McNaughton or your humble servant. At the same time, however, we have to take things as they are, bearing in mind that desirability in so far as it can be attained. In the meantime, what these men have done, many of them, for the last three years-they are not green troops-has been to train in practical manoeuvres and battle drill undfer the most gruelling circumstances, so that they might be fitted as nearly as men can possibly be fitted in rehearsal for actual battle operations.
The term "spearhead" has been frequently used, but it does not necessarily indicate the operation or the role which Canadians will play. The role which Canadians will play will depend upon the circumstances, and upon what those who have1 to do with major strategy in the war will decide, in consultation with the Canadian government and with our military advisers, is the best way in which Canadians can help either as an army or in individual formations.

We in this corner have been sitting patiently all day, saying nothing but listening to a good deal. Some of the things to which we have listened we have regarded as perhaps of considerable value, but there have been other things which, we may have not regarded as so valuable. Perhaps that is all a matter of one's personal opinion. I do not think the government or the minister need be undiuly alarmed if hon. members ask questions with regard to anything. We have a right to expect an answer to these questions.
Somebody this afternoon suggested that the minister should take a train trip some time, sit in the smoker and listen to the conversation of the men. Members of the House of Commons, I believe, live a little closer to the Canadian people than does the minister or the government, and I think we can feel the pulse of public opinion in regard to some of these matters.
I am not going to take up time in discussing Dieppe or Hong Kong, because I frankly confess I do not know much about- it, I have read what the papers have to say and I have certain opinions of my own, but I am not a military strategist and I do not wish to enter where angels fear to tread. I do say, however, that when certain things take place in connection with the war, pass into history and become matters of record, members of the House of Commons have a right to ask for any information they desire with regard to these incidents. We have a right to ask that investigations be carried on in respect of anything we believe it is the public's right to know. We have the right to criticize our war effort. But it is a bit comical to me when hon. members
War Appropriation-Army

rise in their places and state what should be and what should not be done in the way of military strategy. I listened this afternoon to part of the debate and read the report of part of the discussion which it was not my privilege to hear, and I find that hon. members were talking about whether a force should be sent to Alaska or to the Aleutian islands. Well, as far as I am concerned I do not know anything about that, and I doubt whether any other hon. member knows anything about it.
In the first place, we are not provided with all the facts. We do not know how many men are there. So far as I am concerned, and I think in saying this I voice the views of our party, I am willing to leave military strategy with the admirals, the air marshals and the generals, who are trained technicians in matters of warfare. What do we know about it?
But let me add this, that these men have great authority; it is an axiom of logic that with authority comes responsibility; and if, with that authority and responsibility, blunders are made, we have a right to know why, and who is to blame. But until that happens, personally I cannot see a great deal of advantage in discussing whether an army should be sent here or sent there. We are not in possession of the information. When I hear men expressing their opinions on such matters, I turn to the "Parliamentary Guide", and I do not find there any Montgomerys or Alexanders; I do not, I am sure, find any "Eisenhowsers" there. I should have said "Eisenhower"; my hon. friend here confused me; he said that we do not find any Ralstons there, but that is one name we do find in the "Parliamentary Guide".
It may appear that we in this corner of the house are not particularly interested in today's debate on our war effort because we are not -rising in our places every moment and asking something about Dieppe or about some other little bit of military strategy. The fact of the matter is that all one can say in this chamber does not amount to a row of pins in influencing General So-and-so and Admiral So-and-so. Often we hear the cry, "Let us get on with the war"-as though discussing these matters gets on with the war! As a matter of fact, it does not. I am quite certain that those who are in high command, who plan military strategy, do not read what we here are saying.
When it comes to military strategy-and I am not posing as a strategist-if such questions could usefully be asked, there are a number which I should like to bring forward 
The common man in Canada is wondering about some very vital matters. I do not expect an answer to this query which I am about to present, but, as an example, I was talking the other day to a man who said, "I do not understand a lot of things in respect of this war". "Well," I said, "do not come to me and ask me to explain anything about it. Perhaps I am just as confused as you are." He said, "Sometimes I wonder whether it is a game that the nations are playing." "Well, now," I said, "just a moment; do not talk like that, because I would hate to think, with all respect to mothers and fathers who give their sons, that this is a game we are playing." "Well, now," he said

this is the way the common man argues it out-"I would imagine that the best way to gain a victory is to pop off the men who are at the head of things. Adolf Hitler tells the world he is going to meet Mussolini; he tells everybody where he is going to meet him-right in the Brenner pass. We hear of our bombs and blockbusters being dropped over there and wrecking railways and engines. Why do our fliers not go to the Brenner pass and drop bombs there?" We may smile, but so far as I am concerned that man showed1 a good deal of horse sense.
This is a sample of the questions which the average man is inclined to ask. Surely the authorities know where the enemy leaders are once in a while. If we want to wreck German morale, we might do it if we could drop a few thousand tons of bombs in the Brenner pass, wdien wre know the day and the hour Hitler and Mussolini will be there. I do not intend to ask the minister to rise and show me why this is not done. I do not know, but I am quite willing to leave it with the military strategists. I would only repeat that these are the things which the common man is asking.
With respect to military strategy, we have not many strategists here; certainly we have not any who are in possession of all the facts necessary to discuss the subject intelligently. But when it comes to our war effort, or to incidents which are now history and which to the public may appear to be blunders, we have a right to the closest scrutiny of these matters, and those in responsible positions who have made blunders should be taken to task accordingly.

I said this afternoon that about ten minutes would complete on item No. 1 the remarks which I have to make. Inasmuch as the subject of the Dieppe raid has

War Appropriation-Army
been raised since, I wish to say a few words in order to state facts and what we faced, although not in any critical spirit. I am not going to criticize anybody, but I come from a district which, with the surrounding ridings in Toronto, suffered a great deal from casualties incurred in this unfortunate raid. I would not go so far as to blame any member of the government or any officer of the army. But I believe this particular raid must be regarded against a background of the disarmament propaganda which went on for so many years in this country, in Great Britain and elsewhere. You refused to arm on land, on the sea or in the air and threw away your defences. In this particular connection I find that three or four hundred pages of the British Hansard, starting away back last spring, are devoted to criticisms of the British government for the conduct of the war the world over in all theatres. As hon. members know, you Cannot go to war without getting hurt; and we started with a civilian army. We started with a civilian army, started from scratch on land, on sea and in the air, and it took us some time to achieve any results. There was a great deal of criticism last June and July after Mr. Willkie, accompanied by Mr. Fog, made that memorable trip to Russia, round the world in sixty days. All over the world there was a clamour for a second front, coming from those who knew nothing about it and who forgot the great preparations which must be made under conditions of modern warfare. It is a gigantic task to gather the men, equipment, munitions and all the rest of the things that are needed for an action of that kind.
In my opinion it is the duty of an opposition to offer constructive criticism, and that is what I propose to do in the few words I have to say on this subject. Last July, when the war in Africa was going very badly, there was a long discussion for many days in the British House of Commons with regard to mistakes made, and if we had the criticism in Canada that they had over there I am afraid there would be a riot. Member after member got up in the British house; some of them returned from the various theatres of war-admirals, generals, air marshals and all the rest of them-and criticized the way in which the war was being conducted. Mr. Churchill saw fit to move four or five generals, including General Wavell, an all-time military genius, General Auchinleek, General Ritchie and others who had been in charge of the campaign in North Africa; but the war had gone badly for us there because our forces had no equipment. They lacked tanks, anti-tank guns, aeroplanes
and all the rest of it, to do a thing there. Once they obtained proper equipment there was an immediate change.
All this has a direct bearing on this issue. If we go from Africa to the other theatre of war, to Russia and Stalingrad, we find that many changes were made there also. At page 397 of British Hansard Major Markham, a very prominent soldier, is reported to have said:
These officers are perhaps second to none in patriotism, in keenness for their profession and in determination to serve . . .
Then he goes on to say that in Russia-and the same is true of Germany also-they removed staff officers who were in charge of the professional corps of regular officers and replaced them with civilians, who brought about many of the Russian victories in the course of that campaign. On March 31, 1941, a discussion took place in this house between the hon. member for Yale, the hon. member for York-Sunbury and the Minister of National Defence, during which I think the minister gave a very fair statement of the case, setting out the functions of the cabinet in this country, the heads of the army, navy and air force here and those in charge of our' forces in England, in strategy and the conduct of the war. The situation may have changed since that time, but I thought the statement he gave was very good. Part of the discussion was as follows:
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury):	Was it not
really ratified by the Canadian government afterwards?
Mr. Ralston: Hon. members can realize that, on the ground, plans would be made in the expectation that the Canadian government would ratify the judgment of the officer commanding the Canadian corps, if he saw fit to commit his troops; but in connection with one of these matters I have a distinct recollection of communications indicating most clearly that the Canadian government must be consulted with regard to matters of this kind. It is not a case of ratification; it is a case of approval.
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): Beforehand?
Mr. Ralston: Beforehand. I am talking particularly about moving out of England.
Mr. Casselman:	Would that be so if the
governor in council had passed the order in council which is provided for in either section 6 or section 8 of the Visiting Forces Act?
Mr. Ralston: Yes, in my opinion.
I think that is the situation as to strategy and consent to training and use of troops that has obtained ever since.
In connection with the Dieppe raid I should like to quote two or three short paragraphs. First, I should like to refer to the remarks of the Prime Minister of Great Britain as to the reasons for this raid and whether or not it was a military success. Speaking in the House of
War Appropriation-Army

Commons in London on September 8, 1942, on commandos and a second front and invasion of Europe, Mr. Churchill said:
The second important operation was the attack upon Dieppe. It is a mistake to speak or write of this as "a commando raid," although some commando troops distinguished themselves remarkably in it. The military credit for this most gallant affair goes to the Canadian troops, who formed five-sixths of the assaulting force, and to the Royal Navy, which carried them all there and which carried most of them back. The raid must be considered as a reconnaissance in force. It was a hard, savage clash such as are likely to become increasingly numerous as the war deepens. We had to get all the information necessary before launching operations on a much larger scale. This raid, apart from its reconnaissance value, brought about an extremely satisfactory air battle in the west which the fighter command wish they could repeat every week. It inflicted perhaps as much loss upon the enemy in killed and wounded as we suffered ourselves. I, personally, regarded the Dieppe assault, to which 1 gave my sanction, as an indispensable preliminary to full-scale operations. I do not intend to give any information about these operations, and I have only said as much as I have because the enemy can see by his daily reconnaissances of our ports many signs of movements that we are unable to conceal from his photography.
A few months later, on Armistice day, November 11, the Prime Minister clarified what he had said previously and1 put a slightly different construction upon it. That was at a time when Mr. Willkie and Mr. Fog had returned to the United States, and almost everybody else was calling for a second front, without knowing a thing about it or having any military experience in this regard or the reason for the delay. At page 25 of British Hansard for November 11, 1942-this was in the new session, which opened three days before-Mr. Churchill said:
The Russians have borne the burden and the heat of the day, and I think it absolutely natural on their part, and fully within their rights, for them to make the very strong and stark assertions which they have made.
Then, in two sentences, he dealt with the Dieppe raid:
It might have been a relief to our feelings

at least, in the early stages-if we had delivered a premature attack across the channel, if we had had, for instance, a dozen Dieppes on one day and a couple of Dunkirks a week or two later. But a disaster of that character would have been of no help to Russia. It would have been the greatest disservice to Russia.
But the attack which will be made in due course across the channel or the North Sea requires an immense degree of preparation, vast numbers of special landing craft and a great army trained, division by division, in amphibious warfare. All this is proceeding, but it takes time. Of course, should the enemy become demoralized at any moment, the same careful preparations would not be needed.

Risks could be run on a large scale. But this is certainly not the case at the present time. There is a German army in France as large, apart from the home guard, as ours in Great Britain. It is not so well equipped as the British or American troops, but it contains many veteran German soldiers, many experienced officers who have taken part in the overthrow and massacre of a dozen countries. It has ample weapons of the latest type; it has the aid of the immense fortifications erected along the Channel and North Sea coasts. There are also the extraordinary and peculiar difficulties attendant on. all landings across the sea in the teeth of opposition-the chances of weather in this somewhat variable northern climate, the difficulty of reconciling tides and the moons, of catching at one moment high visibility from the air and smooth waters for the landing craft. There are many other factors. I could speak for an hour upon them, but I do not intend to labour the matter, certainly not in public session, because a great many of these difficulties it will be our duty to overcome.
It goes on in this Hansard to refer to conditions in the invasion which were then encountered. A lot has been said and written about the raid'. The Toronto district has been greatly affected in casualties by it, and I have had many letters with regard to it. I have had conversation with several men who were in it. I do not wish to express an opinion, because the casualties were as heavy as were experienced in the last war.
I will say, however, that a great German general has spoken about such raids as this in his textbook,, one of the greatest in Germany. I refer to Marshal von Leeb. I find this in "Crisis in Strategy" in the National Review for November, 1942, at page 401:
Long before this war, von Leeb regarded the problem of defence as of primary importance for the whole of German strategy. In an important manual on the subject von Leeb wrote.
This was a textbook at West Point and at many other military schools long before this war, and the German government in planning their strategy in this war adopted this plan. The quotation continues:
"Let us always remember that attack is the method which decides war and battle. But let us not as a result misread the situation of Germany. Her experiences in the wrorld war of 1914-18, her geographical situation, and the importance of her essentially defensive position emphasize the significance of the defensive within the general development of war."
And he proceeded to develop his ideas in accordance with the lessons which he held that these facts taught. Von Leeb drew on Clause-witz to point the importance of defence, especially when fighting a number of powerful enemies. In that situation, he said, the vital thing is to lose correctly; that is, since to defend everything is to defend nothing, to plan necessary sacrifices so that at the end it is the attacking

War Appropriation-Army
enemy who is at a disadvantage while the defender finishes by rallying himself for successful attack. Von Leeb underlines the importance of this. He writes:
"In particular, everything on all other fronts must be sacrificed so as to bring about a decision in one sector on one front."
And he continues with a complex analysis of the practical problems of defence in terms of tanks, anti-tank guns, aircraft, swift-moving mechanized transport, and such other technological instruments of war as chemical weapons and wireless communications.
A long series 'of allied failures in practicaly every campaign which at one stage or another attempted a sustained offensive against German forces testifies alike to the thoroughness with which the Germans have analysed the problems of modern defence and the efficiency with which they have devised weapons, training and detailed tactics with which to solve those problems.
The names of these gallant but unsuccessful fields are -written in blood in the records of allied warfare. "Knightsbridge" and the "Cauldron" in Libya last June, when 270 British tanks out of 300 were destroyed by the German defences without countervailing tank losses on their side, constitute one example of which we are only too bitterly aware. In Russia, the great German defensive positions at Rhev, Gzhatsk and Sehluesselburg are among the German defensive positions attack on which, though brave, determined, tenacious, and thoroughly organized, has cost our Russian allies only too dear for the results achieved. Our latest experience of the strength of German defences in the west was gained at Dieppe; and Dieppe showed once again that the allies have not yet solved the tactical and operational problems of smashing German defences; problems that must be solved before we can beat the German armed forces; problems that will be solved once we put our full minds and wills into devising their solution.
The recommendation for this raid, or the statement as to who should take part in it was of course the function of the officers in England. A great many men of the city of Toronto were casualties, or were among the missing and! injured. I believe the strategy or plan must have been first submitted in Canada to the war committee of the cabinet, and action taken thereon, as announced by the minister. The minister has replied to the question respecting the survey made of German defences before the raid. I do not know whether he. has seen the leaflet issued here about a month after this raid by the information bureau. However, it was a long sheet of white paper, stating that Yanks were there; they were not and when Mr. Churchill, as shown in Hansard, had said that the Canadians did most of the work and had to.
I should like to quote some further articles in the press handed out, but that would only add to the discomfort of the families of those connected with the raid. Many people have been writing books, and that sort of thing
and propaganda, some of them knowing very little about it. The censor should have stopped it until after the war. A lot of it is not correct.
There has been one criticism however by Admiral Iveyes. His criticism is only partial. In a lecture in England, at Cambridge,, on March 10, 1943, he criticized the conduct of the raid on Dieppe. This British admiral was a former director of combined operations at Zeebrugge and Ostend in the last war. The article, a Canadian Press dispatch, in reporting the lecture states:
Lord Keyes, retired in November, 1941, said he knew "very little about the Dieppe raid except the part played by the 3rd and 4th commandos in their attacks on German batteries on either side of the town." He made no mention of Major General Roberts, commander of a Canadian division, who directed the operation from a ship lying offshore.
He said he thought the plan to land these commandos so close to dawn was running a great risk "since it did not allow for any unforeseen delays, with disastrous results, not only to the 3rd commando but also to the main operation."
"As events proved the main landing at Dieppe against a heavily defended position did not take place early enough to secure the beach and permit the tanks which were timed to land after daylight to make good their landing," Lord Keyes said.
"They were all knocked out by well-sited anti-tank guns which could not be dealt with either from the air or the sea."
He conceded that the fact that more than 300 vessels crossed the Channel through a minefield which had to be swept and that with the exception of one, that carrying the third commando, arrived at their destinations at the appointed times was "greatly to the credit of the navy."
Then, one other article on "Facts of the Raid" from the National Review of last September:
Early on Wednesday, August 19. a combined operations raid was made near Dieppe, when troops and tanks were landed by the Navy under the cover of a powerful air force. The French had been warned by radio that they must keep out of the fight and not expose themselves to German reprisals. The raiding parties were on shore for nine hours. They were composed mostly of Canadians, though there were British, Poles, and Czechs among them. The official .account, gave this picture of the work done.
"It was known that as a consequence of our avowed aggressive policy the Germans had recently been heavily reinforcing the coastal defences of the whole of the occupied territory. Heavy opposition was, therefore, anticipated. In fact it became clear during the raid that the enemy had brought additional troops and guns to the Dieppe area quite recently.
"Despite this heavy opposition, forces were landed on all the beaches together with some tanks. They succeeded in destroying two batteries and the radiolocation station, in-
War Appropriation-Army

flicting heavy casualties upon the enemy forces, in sinking two small _ vessels, and in bringing back a number of prisoners."
This is the first daylight landing we have made in France since the Germans took that country over, and it was successful in its aim and satisfactory as a military exercise. The tanks cruised about the country and streets and the whole operation gave evidence of first-rate staff work.
Once more, as so often happens in our history, the navy held the sea and the army fought across it. But the most important result of the Dieppe raid was that it led to a very large air battle. The official air account is not lengthy and reads:
While the principal objective of the air operations was to give support to the landing and cover to the forces during the land engagement, and to the naval craft, there, in fact, developed one of the greatest air battles of the war. Although this air battle had not been planned as one of the objectives of the operation, the Germans were forced to call up aircraft reinforcements from all parts of occupied France, Holland and Belgium. Many of these enemy aircraft were engaged before they ever reached the area of the operations, large formations being broken up and dispersed particularly over the mouth of the Somme.
During the engagement ninety-one German aircraft are officially known to have been destroyed and about twice that number have probably been destroyed or damaged. In all these operations ninety-eight of our aircraft were lost and the pilots of thirty of these are saved.
The air losses suffered by the enemy temporarily crippled him, and a sweep the next day over northern France to Amiens showed that there were few German fighter aircraft able to fly in that region. The navy took the troops across the narrow seas, waited for them and brought back every possible one of them. One destroyer, H.M.S. Berkeley, was lost, as well as a number of landing craft. The timing went as by clockwork. Only one party was twenty minutes late, and this because they met an enemy convoy and had an encounter with a German armed trawler, which they sank. This delay made for sharp fighting because the element of surprise, in this case, was not present. This particular unit landed under fire. A vivid picture was given in the press of the adventures of Lord Lovat's commando No. 4, and the story reads like a page from Marryat.
The Canadians suffered very heavily. In my opinion there is one unfortunate angle to this particular raid. It seems that we cannot carry on modem warfare without press agents being right up with the troops all the time. They are allowed everywhere. The censors should regulate this better. I believe that many of

the losses would not have occurred if the Germans had not in some way had a tip about the raid. I lost twenty-five of my best friends, many of whom I had known for many years. I do not think it helps to have all these books published, or radio articles or pamphlets. There should be censorship, not only on books but on a great deal of the information given out by some correspondents. Bishop Wells, chief chaplain, said he could not see how war correspondents and press officers could have known all about' the raid from ships outside.
This raid shows that there will have to be another peninsular war in Europe if Germany is to be beaten. She now occupies two-thirds of Europe, and we have not as yet got inside her defences in Europe. If we are to carry out a successful peninsular war, we must regain command of the sea. While it has been predicted by many authorities, I do not think we can win this war alone from the air, without a peninsular war in Europe and the regaining of sea control. The predictions were made two or three years ago that this would be possible, but Germany is yet far from beaten. I am surprised at the way things are going in this country. A red herring, known as social planning, is being drawn across the trail, and the war is now only secondary. I think we should first catch the fox we are hunting before we start after another one, known as social security.
I am sorry for the families of the men in my district who lost their all in this raid. I believe that the disarmament that took place was partly to blame, and the raid) was not worth it. Some mistakes were made in England. I do not think it should be necessary that a man should be a staff college man in order to climb to the top in the army. The minister can correct me if I am wrong, but I believe that this is the case. Germany and Russia even brought in civilians at Stalingrad. Before we can invade Europe we shall have to be prepared and ready for anything that may happen. This war will not be won without an extensive peninsular war, with a year or more of planning. We have had some victories in Africa, but we are now at the darkest and gravest hour of the war. I wish the government every success in carrying out a total war effort. It is the duty of every citizen in Canada to support a total war effort. If the man-power situation had been handled correctly since the war began, and there had been selective service, we would have more men on the front to-day. I am one of those who believe that there is

War Appropriation-Army
no such thing as home defence. We must seek the enemy abroad wherever we can find him, on land, sea or in the air.
I asked the minister whether home defence personnel could be sent to Attu and Kiska islands.
The governor in council has the authority under the act that was passed last year to send them to Attu and Kiska.

Would they be covered by the act as it now stands? The question was raised last night about sending troops to Alaska, and the hon. member for Brantford City suggested that they could be sent to Attu and Kiska. Since he was a government supporter, I questioned1 him. I should like to know now whether the regulations as they at present exist would permit home defence personnel to be sent to Attu and Kiska.
An order in council could be passed under the provisions of the bill passed last year.
That just removed the disabilities. Has there been any general revision of the regulations, or is each case dealt with by a separate order in council?
The orders in council have all been tabled. I do not think there is any order in council covering Attu and Kiska, unless they are included in Alaska.

Is it not
a fact that before any troops can be sent outside the territorial jurisdiction of Canada a special order in council must be passed covering that particular operation?
No, not where the particular place is covered by a general order in council.

Is there
now in process a drafting of the general regulations which would provide authority to send them out without anything more being done?
Not that I know of. We have passed-several orders in council regarding Newfoundland and the United States and Alaska.
