speechtext: Shall item No. 1 carry?
Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The next item is pay
and allowances, $539,730,211.

I should like to
ask the minister a question arising out of an article which appeared in the press a short time ago. It reads:	.
Basic Training
A soldier's wife with a husband three years overseas says she, and many of her friends in similar status, neveF received any increase in pay when the soldiers on this side of the water got a raise to $1.50 a day.
She writes: "I have been told that they do not figure our men have had basic training. Can you tell me when they are likely to get basic training if they have not had it after three and a half years of service? I should be very pleased if you could put us all straight on this matter."
Many people are wondering why these men have not received this increase in pay, and I know some of the men overseas find it difficult to understand this.

When the minister
answers that question I wonder if he could give us the information which he told me the other day he had with respect to the percentage of men, both overseas and in Canada, who have received this raise. He will recall that we had some difficulty in getting the question worded properly.

The question just asked
is along the same line as the one asked by the hon. member for St. Paul's. Here is what I have in regard to Canada. A survey was made covering 187,000 troops. The survey is not complete, but it ought to be a fair indication of the percentage throughout. Of those who have had four months training, 27-8 per cent are still receiving $1.30 a day.
Are the overseas men receiving $1.30 a day?

I will come to that in a moment. Then 18-6 per cent of those who have served four months are receiving $1.40 a day, and 53-6 per cent are receiving $1.50 a day. That is, 72-2 per cent

18 -6 plus 53-6 per cent-of the number who have served for four months out of the group in respect of which the check was made are receiving either SI.40 or $1.50 a day. It may be that those receiving $1.40 a day have not served the additional two months, but I cannot say as to that.
Answering my hon. friend's question about overseas men, I can give roughly these figures. We telegraphed Canadian military headquarters, and they took a test check of certain units, in order to give the information back promptly to us, which they thought would be indicative. The telegram we have received is that between 80 and 85 per cent-I think it was
War Appropriation-Army

a little more than 85 per cent-of those who have served four months are receiving the increase in pay, and about the same percentage for those who have served over six months. I would like any cases that hon. members have in hand brought to my attention so that I can wire the names over. I want to ascertain what has gone wrong. We had communications by wire some time ago. There was a little delay in dealing with the matter in some of the units, and we wired indicating clearly that we desired the utmost expedition to be used in having the increase in pay put into effect as rapidly as possible.

I had quite a number of communications about this very matter, but on analysis I came to the conclusion that my inquirers did not thoroughly understand the regulations. I could well understand that when I came to see and read the regulations for myself, because there were a good many conditions precedent to obtaining the increased pay. On explaining that to my correspondents I found that in ninety per cent of the cases some one or more than one of the necessary conditions had not been fulfilled. I think in fairness to the national defence department that ought to be stated.

What are the conditions? Here is the case of a man who has been overseas for three years. He had a clean sheet until just three months before this increase came into effect, and he did not get the increase. I do not think anybody can understand why that would be.
I am sorry that I have not the regulations with me, but I shall be glad to give them to the committee to-morrow.
That would be a good idea.
Do the draftees get the increased pay, too?

Yes. I think there has been a little misunderstanding about the increased pay. When the increased pay was put into effect applying to the army it was intended to be along the lines of the increased pay which was given in the air force to the AC2 who becomes AC1 after three months service and becomes LAC. after six months' service. Under the air force regulations the commanding officer decides whether the increase is merited having regard to the training of the man and the degree of proficiency he has attained. Men in the air force are reclassified as AC1 after three months, and there is another reclassification after six months. In the army the increase is made after four months, instead of three, because there was a definite break at the

end of four months; that is to say, the man was supposed to be taking basic training which would be completed in four months. But there has been this difficulty, and these are probably the cases that hon. members have in mind, that some men have not had basic training at basic training centres and passed the test expressly provided. So that we have provided a fifty-hour course which enables a man on passing to qualify, notwithstanding the fact that he does not strictly come within the letter of the regulations which my hon. friend saw. I presume those were the printed regulations.
The minister sent me a copy.

There is a provision that if the man takes that fifty-hour course and passes, that is compliance with the conditions which are required with reference to basic training. There is a further provision applying to the older men, the veterans, who are not in a position to take the same sort of strenuous training as the younger men. We have made special provision for them. I wish to impress on the committee that there is a degree of proficiency required in connection with increased pay.
And good conduct?
Yes, and good conduct. If there has been a forfeiture of three days pay within the four months, they do not get the increase until there is a clear conduct sheet for the required period.

That is a fairly
severe penalty for a minor offence. Here is a case of a man who has been overseas for three years and had a clear sheet, and just because of that forfeiture he does not get the increase. That is rather serious.
It is not so serious. He has to have a clean conduct sheet for a clear four months.
He has to begin all over again for the four months.
That is all. There are three conditions: (1) length of service; (2) good conduct, and (3) a certain degree of proficiency.

May I ask a question with respect to the men who have an opportunity of taking the fifty-hour course? Is it fair to make them wait? Men have come back from overseas and cannot understand why they should not get the increased pay. They have been overseas but have not had

War Appropriation-Army
basic training. When they come back they cannot understand why they should not have had the increased pay long before this, but they cannot get increased pay. Why should the increased pay not be made retroactive to some reasonable date?

I must say that I have not had a word of complaint from overseas. Canadian military headquarters were satisfied that the increase was being paid to all those who were entitled. We took pains to have Canadian military headquarters understand that they were not to be reluctant about granting increased pay but rather to assist the men in every way possible to qualify for it. There is nothing niggardly about it at all. We are giving the trained soldier badge, notwithstanding the objection of some hon. member to badges, to a man along the same lines as the LAC. badges are given in the air force. The increased pay implies training as well as service. A man getting a badge has a certain amount of pride in it, and it is also better for the army.

Under this item I should like to support one thing which the minister said when giving his report to the committee. He said that while basic pay of women was lower than that of men, consideration was being given to the question of training pay being on the same basis and of granting dependents' allowance to women. I would urge not only that consideration be given to the question of having equal pay for various trades, but also that the whole question of basic pay for women be put forward as a basis of equality with that of men in the armed forces.
I was hoping, some time during the discussion of the war appropriations, to be able to review fairly generally the position of women in this country in our war effort, but under this special item I cannot go farther than women in the auxiliary services. The question of women in other fields will have to be left to some other time. However, what I have to say to-night will apply also to the women's auxiliary services in other departments.
I think it is significant that the position of women in the various countries of the world is indicative of their state of progress. We have looked upon countries such as prerevolutionary China, czarist Russia and India as backward countries, and they are countries where the position of women has been deplorable. We have noticed also that in the fascist countries, where formerly the people had some degree of democracy and of equality, the position of women has been pushed back.
On the other hand, in the very opposite direction, there is one country, the Soviet Union, where to-day the position of women is far superior to that of the women of any other nation, for women there are granted absolute equality, economic, social, political and cultural with the men. It will be agreed also that the equality granted to women in the Soviet Union has been responsible for their remarkable development, because not only have the women in that country made a very great contribution to its progress during the last twenty-five years, but recently the women of Russia have produced many heroines in the defence of their country, and this has well justified that equality which they have been given. With regard to Canada and the United1 States, women are supposed to have equality with men, but on an economic basis they have not yet achieved it.
I think it will be agreed that the emancipation of women is something for which we yet have to strive. We would not have had that political equality we have to-day had it not been for the suffragette movement in Britain. So far as I am concerned, I do not suffer from any discrimination in that respect. So far as the women members go, we do not receive two-thirds of the indemnity given to the men, but that is something of an accident. It is possible that the fathers of confederation, in their wildest dreams and flights of fancy, never thought for a moment that women would encroach upon their prerogative, so that, when women came to the House of Commons, they entered on a basis of equality with men. Had it been otherwise, I would have started a union of the women members of the house, and I am sure that with the support of the other woman member I would have striven for equality, not only on our own account but by reason of the principle involved, and on behalf of other women who will be sitting in this house some day in the future.
With regard to women in the auxiliary services, we as a nation have called on these young women to take up a great responsibility, and they are doing an excellent job. The minister himself has admitted it. They have gone into offices and various departments and have taken the places vacated by men, and they are doing the work as efficiently as the men did. On that basis I fail 'to see why it is that women in the auxiliary services receive only two-thirds of the basic pay. I fail to see how it is that we have arrived at that situation or why it has not been remedied during the period we have had women in the auxiliary services.
War Appropriation-Army

As regards the question of young women receiving dependents' allowances, I have reliable information about the women's services in Britain. There, if a young woman can prove that before joining up she had made a contribution to her parents, it is possible for her to have an allowance. I submit that we should very quickly see that the same applies to the young women here. We have overcome in the past fairly well the discrimination with regard to religion and race, though not altogether, but we still do suffer in this country from sex discrimination, and at the present time there is a great need for us to take stock of this question and eliminate the discrimination and give to the women of the country full equality when we ask them to do an equal job with the men in various directions, for the girls in the army are doing a wonderful job.
I have heard it said that men arrive at their decisions by reason and logic and that women more often rely on intuition and their emotions, but I fail to see what logic is behind the position where women receive only two-thirds of the basic pay which men receive, when the women do the same job. If the minister can explain the logic behind that, I shall be glad to know what it is, because I appreciate logic. I believe it is a hang-over, a relic of the past, of the dark ages, which has hung on to us, relegating women to a position of inferiority. The men have said, "We are glad to accept you, but we cannot pay you the same as we pay the men." Why? I say this to the minister honestly: When we women have discarded the old Victorian red flannel petticoat to do the job, it is time the men discarded the red flannel petticoats around their minds and gave us equality. Nothing would do more to encourage young women to take on the responsibility which they are asked to shoulder than to be given equality with the men, and I urge the minister not to waste time in discussing the matter. There is nothing to discuss; simply go ahead and grant them equality in basic pay and other privileges.

The thought that has been in my mind, which prompts me to speak on this subject, is rather the converse of what the hon. member who has just spoken has suggested. It is true that the criticism I have finds its origin probably in pre-Victorian days. An officer in his majesty's army was expected perforce to marry a lady of means who was able to provide for herself, because it seems a strange anomaly that not only in the army but in the air force an officer is not obliged by law or by the regulations to provide for

his wife. A private, corporal, sergeant, sergeant-major, a non-commissioned officer on entering the Canadian army-and I believe the same applies to Britain-is required by the regulations to assign so many days' pay to his wife and dependent children or dependents as the case may be. But perforce, when he becomes a commissioned officer, the same obligation does not obtain.
This has been brought forcibly to my attention in one particular instance I have in mind. That was some months ago, and in the interim seven or eight additional cases have been drawn to my attention. During my recent visit home I learned of five or six others, wherein, thanks to the new idea of promotions within the forces, men have risen from the ranks and are now commissioned officers. But the one instance of which I have intimate personal knowledge is that of a man who enlisted as a private, having a wife and two children; he became a commissioned officer and forthwith cancelled his assigned pay; or rather the assignment was no longer operative by reason of his promotion, and his wife and dependent children are worse off to the extent of between $40 and $50 a month. It is my understanding that in numerous cases commissioned officers in the Canadian army have stopped their assigned" pay and that all their wives and dependent children have to live on is what they receive from the dependents' allowance board; whereas these same men, or men equally valiant, if non-commissioned officers or private soldiers, would have to make assignments before the dependents' allowance was paid to their wives and children.
My observations apply not only to the army but equally to the air force, where the same rule applies. A married man with a family, upon being commissioned, is no longer ' required by rule, regulation or law to assign any portion of his pay to his wife. A number of Canadian wives of officers find themselves poorer by reason of their husbands' promotion to commissioned rank.
There is another phase of this matter of which I speak with some hesitation in this chamber, and only because I have made repeated representations to the authorities. We have in this country numbers of members of the Royal Air Force taking training. Some of these men, two or three of whom I know personally, upon completing their course were commissioned as officers of the Royal Air Force and retained in this country as instructors in that force. Facilities were provided whereby such of these men who are married were enabled to bring their wives to this

War Appropriation-Army
country. I believe these officers receive the same pay and allowances as similar ranks in the Royal Canadian Air Force. In two instances of which I have personal knowledge, when the wife arrived from the old land she was told that her husband no longer cared for her. The assigned pay was stopped; and two very charming English ladies found themselves five thousand miles from home, dependent entirely upon the dependents' allowance paid by the Canadian government. I say that the principle is wrong. I have contended and still contend that if there is a rule which is justified in equity and sound logic that a non-commissioned officer or man must assign a certain portion of his pay to his dependents, there is no rhyme or reason why, if that man becomes a commissioned officer, the same law should not apply; at least he should be obliged to assign a definite minimum of his monthly pay, and it is not good enough to allow any man to be so remiss in his duties as to refrain from providing for his wife and dependent children and to release him from the obligation of doing so. I protest against such a situation being allowed to continue.
We may be informed, perhaps, by some of the "higher-ups" in the air force and the army that "after all, this fellow is a good soldier; we are not concerned so much about his morals or his domestic troubles or problems; and anyway, there is no legal process whereby you can compel a man to recognize his obligations to his wife and children." That is something which should be remedied, and I hope it will be remedied by the Minister of National Defence and the other ministers associated with him in charge of our active fighting force. If it is not done, I should like to know on what basis or for what reason a commissioned officer is permitted to avoid making provision for his wife and dependents when a non-commissioned officer or a private is compelled or obliged to do so.

First, with regard to the case made by the hon. member for North Battleford. I do not think there is anything to-night which I can add to what I have said in the passage which she quoted. As I said, the matter is under active consideration. I hesitate to guess why it is that the pay was different. I could make a couple of speculations about it, although I know the hon. member will not regard] either reason, as sufficient. One is, I think, that the similar 'body in England have the same gradations of pay, and that when the women's services were formed here they were modelled after the ATS and the same differential in pay was made. The only other point which
I can think of at the minute is that it is true, as the hon. member will realize, that women are not in combatant work; that is, that there is not every place in the army where they can serve, as men can. She may think that is a bit of red flannel petticoat wrapped round the masculine mind1, but at the same time those who drafted the regulations in the first place may have felt it formed some basis for making the rate of pay different. As I have said in my statement, active consideration is being given, regardless of whether there may be a difference in the basic rate of pay, to the point that trades pay for doing the same work should be the same for a woman as for a man; that is, that the differentiation should not be carried farther.
Is the whole question not one of equality of service?

Yes. I assume that those who made the differentiation in the first place considered there was some difference in that women cannot serve in all types of soldiering. But I assure my hon. friend that what she has said to-night will have attention. I am tremendously sympathetic with anything which may promote esprit de corps, and which may indicate appreciation of the work which the women are doing. I spoke particularly of the CWAC, but it applies also to the women's division of the ah' force and of the navy as well. I greatly appreciate the work they are doing, and the way in which they are taking men's places in a great many jobs. I have no hesitation in repeating what I have said in other places, that in the jobs they are taking over they are doing as well as the men whom they are releasing, if not better.
With reference to what was said by the hon. member for Calgary West, I was not in on the making of the dependents' allowance regulations, and I cannot tell him why there is no requirement that an officer shall assign part of his pay before he is entitled to dependents' allowance for his wife. Nevertheless that is the regulation. There is this to be said, that the wife of a lieutenant gets $45 in separation allowance as compared wdth $35 for the wife of a man in the ranks, and I believe the rate for the wife of an officer of higher rank goes up to $60 a month. I have every sympathy with the case that has been made out by the hon. member, and I say to him, as I said to the hon. member for North Battleford with regard to her case, that the matter is under active consideration now, and that as a matter of fact an amendment has been drafted on that very point. I do not
War Appropriation-Army

know that it will go to the full extent my hon. friend wants, but I am satisfied1 that if and when it is approved it will be sufficient to take care of cases of the sort to which he has referred. I must say that I am rather reluctant to have the army interfere in the domestic or financial relations between husband and wife; it seems to me the rule should apply that the employer ought to keep out of it. However, we have done it in connection with the men, and it seems to me there may be justification for doing it in respect to officers as well, in necessary cases.

What
about the case I mentioned this afternoon, of the man who has volunteered and gone overseas, leaving a wife and child in Canada? In the courts of Britain he is found guilty of a crime, and punished. The woman is automatically cut off; her whole source of revenue is gone. It seems to me that is a terrible hardship, and one which this country should seek to meet at least in part. I know of a particular case-
Is that the case of a chap getting into trouble over there?

Yes, and
there was an automatic cessation of pay and allowances to the wife and children. The family are living on charity.

In that case the provision
is this. If it is a case of detention or imprisonment or penal servitude-I do not know whether that is the case-
That is it.

-where the detention or imprisonment is for a period of six months or more, payments of dependents' allowance and assigned pay cease at the date of discharge of the soldier from the force or at the expiration of six months from the date of sentence, whichever is the earlier. Of course my hon. friend would not object to the allowance ceasing at the time of discharge from the forces; obviously you cannot keep on paying dependents' allowance after that. In the case of a soldier detained and still kept on the strength, however, the dependents' allowance does not Gease until the expiration of six months from the date of sentence. I am wondering if in that particular case the six months have elapsed.
I have not the correspondence here.
Would the hon. gentleman give me the name of the case?
I will try to find it.

I wish to touch on the subject to which the hon. member for York-Sunbury has just referred and which was brought up last night by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, namely, the plight of women who have been receiving dependents' allowance and assigned pay, when their husbands go absent without leave or commit some other misdemeanour and get into trouble. I have a case that I have been taking up with the dependents' allowance board within the last few days. I am informed by the board that if the man is overseas, the dependents' allowance and assigned pay is continued for two months instead of twenty-one days.
For three months on the first occasion he goes absent without leave. If he goes absent again, the allowance is continued for only two months.

I imagine this was rather a bad case; the man had been imprisoned, and I think since July, 1942, he has been away without leave most of the time. I have a letter from the dependents' allowance board from which I should like to read some paragraphs in reference to the point I wish to make. On this occasion this man has been absent without leave since February 28, 1943, and I am told that the dependents' allowance was continued until April 28, 1943.
That must have been the second time he was absent.
I imagine that may be so.
Apparently he does not like the army.

There is a peculiar proviso, in this letter, considering the circumstances. The chairman of the board says:
We are sorry that we are unable to make further payments on this account until such time as he returns to his unit. The regulations provide that dependents' allowance is payable only until the 21st day of absence but in cases where the soldier is overseas it is continued for a _ longer period to provide for any possible mistake in information received.
Then comes the proviso to which I have referred:
It is necessary, however, to recover any payments made beyond the 21st day if it subsequently appears that the soldier was actually absent without leave.
In the case I brought to the attention of the board it would be quite impossible to recover anything that had been paid, unless it was held back from future allowances. This woman has two children, aged

War Appropriation-Army
three and four. She has tried every means to keep the family together. She went to work in a restaurant at $48 a month and boarded the children, for which she had to pay $24 a month. She found it impossible to carry on and had to give up her work. She would have carried on in that way but for the fact that the people boarding the children would not continue to do so for the amount she was paying.
It seems to me that to allow a situation of this kind to continue is really bad; I do not know whether you would say it was bad for morale; but it creates a bad atmosphere; it interferes with recruiting and all that sort of thing. Surely there cannot be so many cases of this kind that better provision could not be made for the wives and children. I wanted to bring this particular case to the attention of the minister, not because the hon. member for Cape Breton South did not present the matter very well last night but because this is such a useless way of dealing with the situation that I really think something should be done about it.

I should like to make a suggestion with respect to insurance, because this would seem to be the proper place to make it. The United States army has what I think is a very good provision, in that when the soldier passes through the induction centre he is offered the choice of taking either $5,000 or $10,000 insurance at a particularly low rate. I have not the figures as to rates before me, but one of the officers told me that he was taking $10,000 worth of insurance, and that his payments each month were only $5 or $6. That is a great deal lower rate than that offered by any commercial company.
It was emphasized that this insurance gave the individual soldier a great feeling of security. It made him feel that in the event' of his becoming a casualty this insurance money would become payable; that he would know the government or the state would look after his dependents, and that a fund would be available, without necessity of going to a pension board, or having any type of red tape. He would feel that he had life insurance on him which would be automatically payable. I was informed that this was one of the greatest morale-building provisos, and particularly as it applied to the newly inducted soldier. I would ask the minister to bring down the figures, if he can get them, with respect to the United States insurance plan, and some indication as to whether a similar plan could be introduced into the Canadian army.
I should like to make a further statement with regard to dependents' allowances with respect to men undergoing detention. I was informed, and I believe correctly, that the dependents of a soldier in the United Kingdom forces, irrespective of the length of his sentence, so long as he is still in the service, and is confined in a military prison, continue to receive the benefits. Those payments are carried on until he is discharged from the service. I was informed that that was considered to be a beneficial proviso in the regulations. It seems rather hard that a wife should be made to suffer, after a six months' period, in the event of her soldier husband being arrested for some serious crime, and sentenced to one or two years penal servitude. I suggest that the department give this matter careful consideration.
Then, a number of soldiers have been lost in England, and are now classified either as deserters or as being absent without leave. My own unit happened to be in Liverpool during a bad blitz on the Merseyside, which took place in 1940, and later in 1941, and naturally went out to help the fire-fighters and the air raid protection forces. After one or two of the raids several men from my unit were posted as missing. I was informed it was not known whether the men had been killed in the raid, and their bodies totally burned and therefore absolutely unrecognizable and unidentifiable, or whether they had gone absent without leave. I understand the regulation is that if a man does not present himself for duty after a certain period of time, he is classified as being absent without leave. It may be that there are a number-I do not know how great the number would be, but the department may have some estimate of it-of men who have been killed, really on active service, but who are now classified either as deserters or as being absent without leave.

The hon. member for York-Sunbury and the hon. member for Vancouver South have referred to the striking off of dependents' allowances and assigned pay as they apply to wives whose husbands are deserters. I have in mind a case similar to that mentioned to-night by the hon. member for Vancouver South.
That is the case of a mother of two children, one of one and a half years of age and the other three years old. Her husband, after being in the army for some time, deserted. This lady was thrown on to the hospitality of the Red Cross in Calgary. That organization has taken the stand that it is not their responsibility. Under the circumstances she cannot get a job, because the
War Appropriation-Army

children are too small to leave. She cannot obtain a position which would bring her sufficient income to enable her boarding the children out. For these reasons her situation is an impossible one.
This lady is not responsible for her husband's desertion. The department takes the stand that on account of this desertion she cannot receive assigned pay, or any allowance from the dependents' allowance board. Apparently she did receive pay for twenty-one days. She is absolutely helpless, as a result of the position taken by the Red Cross. Surely some consideration should be given to her. There should be some means by which she can receive compensation. In a case of dire necessity, where a woman is helpless, is there not some chance of her receiving pay on compassionate grounds?

There is section 119, but I cannot tell my hon. friend' how far it goes. It provides for a reference to the treasury board, in respect of special cases. That is the only section I know of, unless it came under the jurisdiction of the dependents' board of trustees. I shall make an inquiry.

I received a letter a few days ago from a soldier who has been in England for more than two years, inquiring about the increase in pay of twenty cents a day. How long must they be over there to receive that increase? I was' under the impression that it was a blanket regulation, covering every soldier serving overseas, no matter what length of time. I understood that they received $1.50 instead of $1.30.
I dealt with that matter in reply to a question asked by another hon. member. I do not know whether the hon. member was in the chamber.
I was here, yes.

There are three qualifications, the first of which is four months service. The second is efficiency; that is to say, a certain degree of efficiency must be established. The original provision was that a man should have completed his basic training in accordance with the standard syllabus. That was found to be too much of a hardship in certain cases where men had not had the standard syllabus, and provision has been made to give them what I might call condensed1 courses in jorder that they may qualify. Even this has been modified in the case of older soldiers. Then the third thing is conduct; that is to say, entries on the conduct sheet which provide for deductions of pay exceeding a total of three days' pay. When the conduct sheet

shows such an entry it is not regarded as a clean conduct sheet. A man must serve for four months without an entry of that kind. Those are the three grounds.
The matter has been brought to the attention of the overseas authorities. The figures I gave the committee to-night were that about eighty to eighty-five per cent, according to a test taken of a certain number of units, have already been awarded the increased pay. I am particularly interested in having names that might come to the attention of hon. members, because there may be isolated instances where some unit or some formation has disregarded, perhaps unintentionally or perhaps through a misunderstanding of the regulations, following out what should be done. I took special pains to participate in the drafting of the telegram that went to Canadian military headquarters in regard to this matter when it seemed that there was some slowness in getting things through.

Will the minister state
whether any consideration has been given or will be given in the future to making the increase to $1.50 a day automatic throughout the ranks affected? It has been stated by the hon. member for Eraser Valley and others that it came as a surprise to learn that this increase was not automatic. Information given to me in reply to a question I asked on May 6 was to the effect that although the increase from $1.30 to $1.50 a day had certain conditions attached to it-'the minister has recited them two or three times to-night-nevertheless in the case of lance-corporals and lance-bombardiers the increase from $1.50 to $1.60 was automatic. This answer appears on page 2429 of Hansard. My contention is that that is good, but the same principle should be applied to the other ranks referred to, such as troopers, gunners, sappers and privates.

The principle is altogether different. The lance-bombardier or the lance-corporal has already shown his efficiency by getting his stripe. The increase from $1.50 to $1.60 a day is made in order to maintain the differential. Otherwise there would be no inducement for a man to try to get corporal's stripes. His efficiency has been shown, or he would not have his stripes.

I maintain that the
differential is established by the difference between $1.60 and $1.50. It seems to me that $1.50 is a low enough minimum to have applied throughout all ranks. I feel that penalizing a man in this way is unfair; that is, penalizing for infractions of one kind or another. I would hope the minister could

War Appropriation-Army
give some indication that consideration! will be given to making $1.50 a day the minimum in the Canadian army.

There has been quite a
battle in connection with getting this $1.50. I do not want the idea to get abroad1 that men are being penalized. This rate has existed in the air force for some time. I was one of those who felt that soldiers required the same qualifications as airmen. It seemed to me that if they were proficient and efficient they should get this recognition. I wish to be quite frank and state that the airmen's regulation is not as specific as the army regulation with regard to qualifications, but it does indicate that there must be proficiency and worthiness. The worthiness idea has to do with conduct.
Is a man who has committed a minor crime debarred?

No; but I understand that good conduct is one of the things to which the commanding officer looks. Air force administrative order No. D.44-2 reads:
16. Except in the case of direct enlistment under special authority and provided the reclassification is within the limit for the trade as shown in table "A", without higher authority a commanding officer may-
(a)	Reclassify	an	aircraftman	class	2	to
class 1, when he is satisfied that the airman is proficient in service duties, worthy of advancement and has completed a minimum of three months' service since enlistment.
In the army it is four months instead of three.
(b)	Reclassify	an	aircraftman	class	1	to
leading aircraftman when he is satisfied that the airman is proficient in service duties, worthy of advancement and has completed a minimum of three months' service since being reclassified to aircraftman class 1.
In order to indicate that there is no hard and fast rule and that we adopt the air force standard, namely, the opinion of the commanding officer as to a man's proficiency, we say in connection with the second increase in pay:
The soldier must have attained a degree of proficiency in training applicable to his arm or corps which ought to be reached two months after completion of basic training. The officer commanding must be satisfied as to degree of proficiency attained by the soldier before increase is authorized.
I suggest that they are along exactly the same lines. There is no suggestion of its being automatic in either case. It may be that there are more words in connection with the army or that it is a little stiffer; but the same objective is being sought, namely, that a man should receive some recognition for
having taken the time and pains to prepare himself as a soldier and to carry on as we would like a soldier to carry on.

Would the
minister read the provisions with respect to good conduct?

They are the same in
both cases and they read:
(a) Conduct. When during the preceding four-month period, entries on his field conduct sheet entailing penal deductions of pay as defined in section 138, subsections (1) and (2) of the Army Act do not in the aggregate exceed a total of three days' pay or in the case of fines do not exceed an amount equal to three days' pay or the sum total of entries do not exceed an amount equal to three days' pay.
That is to say, if he has not been penalized to the extent of losing more than three days' pay in the four month period he would be eligible. The same applies with regard to conduct in connection with the second increase. This reads:
The soldier will be eligible provided he fulfils the conditions as defined in paragraph 2(a) above during the two-month period following the first increase.
He would be penalized already under the terms of the regulations the minister has just read, and this in fact would be a further penalty through the man being debarred from the increase.
I did not quite catch what my hon. friend said, and I should like to understand him.

The point is that the soldier who has been guilty of something for which he has lost a few days pay, not only pays for his misconduct in that way but pays a further penalty through being debarred from an increase.

That is a doctrine which is promulgated in the department quite often, more particularly in connection with officers rather than men. I am told-I am speaking quite frankly to the committee-that an officer who has been court-martialled and reprimanded severely should be sent right back to his job just the same as before. They say that he is being penalized if he is not allowed to go back to his same job. I say that that man may suffer another penalty on account of the fact that when he has been convicted and has had to be reprimanded he cannot do the job he did before. I am saying the same about the soldier. If he happens to have a lapse involving three days pay he has to wait a little longer. I do not regard it as a double penalty at all. He must qualify for the increased pay; that is all.
War Appropriation-Army
Once he has qualified, will he be deprived of the pay if he commits another crime?
No.
He does not revert again?
No, not at all'.

The minister is hardly
correct in saying there is not a double penalty. But in his opinion the double penalty is deserved.
I do not say that it is a double penalty. I say that if he fails to qualify he does not get the increase in pay.

From the percentage the minister gave, I take it that there would be a considerable number of men overseas who have not qualified for the increase even though they have been overseas for a considerable time.
I gave the percentages just as I got them, from 80 to 85 per cent.

In other words, from 15 to 20 per cent of the men overseas who have been there for a considerable time have not qualified. Can the minister tell us on which ground they failed to qualify? Was it lack of good conduct or inefficiency?

My	hon. friend has
brought something else to my memory. There were, in addition, about six per cent in each class who were qualified for the increased pay but who had not yet actually received it. The paymaster had1 not got around to it, I understand. That brings the percentage up to around 90 per cent in the units in which the test was made, which were regarded as average units. But, meeting my hon. friend's question, that still leaves about ten per cent in those test units who have not qualified. I cannot give my hon. friend the reason, but I hope to have that information.
Was it lack of good conduct or inefficiency?
I am sorry I cannot tell my hon. friend. This was the information we got from Canadian military headquarters in a four-line paragraph giving the result of the test check.
It would be well to make the percentage 100.

Can the minister tell us if there is any appreciable

number of men overseas who are absent without leave? I have heard rather disquieting reports that the number was substantial. Perhaps the minister would let us have that information to-morrow. It is quite apparent that we cannot finish this part of the discussion to-night. I understand the minister wants to put the regulations on Hansard, so that hon. members who have not read them may do so.
It would perhaps meet the convenience of hon. members and save much discussion if I put them on Hansard now.

Just before the minister does that, I have three other questions, in addition to the question I asked which the minister said he would take as a notice to produce.
First, how many men have been discharged or struck off strength from the Canadian active army from the beginning of the war to the end of the present fiscal year, March 31?
Second, how many men have been discharged or struck off strength from the home defence force? I understand that is the draftees.

We are compiling that now, but it is not yet complete. The records were kept in a separate branch of the records office. I have questioned myself why we did not know exactly how many men had been discharged. But that information will be available later.
My third question is this: How many home defence men are there serving in the Canadian army; that is, men who are not available for service anywhere outside Canada?

I wish to ask a question with respect to the dependents' allowance. I would direct the minister's attention to the case of a married man who deserts his wife and family, enlists, then takes unto himself another wife and after a time becomes the father of another family. In this case I understand he is at liberty-
Not much liberty there.

I understand he is at liberty to sign over a certain portion of his pay and the dependents' allowance to the common-law wife and leave to the mercy of the world his legal wife and children. I am wondering whether this is a square deal and what can be done about it.

War Appropriation-Army
I will make a note of it and bring it to the notice of the dependents' allowance board.

May I make one observation with respect to that matter? It always seems to me, on the basis of such cases as are brought forward by the member for Rattle River, that the fight we have to make is on behalf of the legal wife. Apparently the authorities are willing to recognize the common-law wife and the children of that relationship, if there are any. Perhaps all these cases should be reviewed. I am certainly of the opinion that the legal wife should be given all possible protection. After all, the common-law wife, the adulteress, knows that she is not deserving of any great amount of consideration. I certainly think she should not have any until the legal wife is properly taken care of first.

May I now put on record the regulations regarding increases of pay as requested by the hon. member for York-Sunbury, and added to that should be the statement that special provision has been made for qualification through condensed courses by which men may qualify for basic training. That is provided in connection with the first four months of service. The regulations are as follows:
C.A.R.O. No. 2772 sets forth governing conditions as follows:
First increase after four months' continuous service-
(a)	Conduct
When during preceding four-month period entries on his field conduct sheet entailing penal deductions of pay as defined in section 138 subsections (1) and (2) of the Army Act do not in the aggregate exceed a total of three days' pay or in the ease of fines do not exceed an amount equal to three days' pay or the sum total of entries do not exceed an amount equal to three days' pay.
(b)	Efficiency
The soldier must have completed basic training in accordance with "The Standard Syllabus for Basic Training" and have qualified in all tests as laid down in M.F.M. 105 (X).
Second increase after six months' continuous service-
(a)	Conduct
The soldier will be eligible provided he fulfils the conditions as defined in para. 2 (a) above during the two-month period following the first increase.
(b)	Proficiency
The soldier must have attained a degree of proficiency in training applicable to his arm or
corps, which ought to be reached two months after completion of basic training. The officer commanding must be satisfied as to degree of proficiency attained by the soldier before increase is authorized.
